SpaceX, Tesla explore possible merger
(CNN)– Elon Musk says SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to explore a merger.
Musk, who is ceo of both companies, was speaking on a SpaceX earnings call Tuesday (October 20).
He said he thinks there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies.
The remarks appeared to be the most forceful ones Musk has made publicly about a potential merger.
Musk said as a “conflicting party,” he can’t be part of the discussions.
He said it’s ultimately up to the special shareholder committees from each company.

sources.news_title: A SpaceX-Tesla megamerger could benefit both companies and Elon Musk’s personal fortune
Elon Musk plans to merge SpaceX and Tesla in a $3.6 trillion deal
sources.text:
SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk is considering bringing the two companies together into a single entity spanning rockets, satellites, internet services, chatbots, social media, robots and cars, according to the billionaire’s comments.
Musk said Tuesday that both companies had established special committees of independent directors to study a potential merger, which he described as “a good idea.” However, he acknowledged that, as a major shareholder and executive at both companies, he would be a “conflicted party” and cautioned that there was no guarantee the two sides would reach an agreement.
READ: Tesla faces lawsuit after fatal Texas autopilot crash (June 24, 2026)
If the deal goes ahead, the combined entity would be valued at about $3.6 trillion, placing it among the world’s five most valuable companies, alongside Nvidia, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft.
However, the deal would face several hurdles, including shareholder concerns over Musk’s influence and regulatory approval. SpaceX shares surged 9% in early trading Wednesday, while Tesla stock rose 2.5%.
According to analyst forecasts compiled by Visible Alpha, the combined company would employ more than 155,000 people and generate $153 billion in revenue this year. However, analysts also expect it to have negative free cash flow of at least $54 billion, as Musk’s spending plans for AI infrastructure, chip fabrication plants and rockets continue to expand.
The deal would also strengthen Musk’s control over Tesla. He controls about 84% of the voting rights at SpaceX through super-voting shares, compared with roughly 20% at Tesla, where each share carries one vote.
Analysts predict that Tesla will sell more than 500,000 Model 3 sedans, more than 1 million Model Y vehicles and 22,000 Cybertrucks this year. The company also has a growing self-driving business and an Optimus humanoid robot program that Musk has predicted could eventually help make Tesla worth $25 trillion.
Musk said Tuesday that a merger made sense because “we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” referring to the point at which AI surpasses human intelligence. His remarks appeared to signal that AI is a central priority for the billionaire.
READ: Tesla driver assistance probe closed after minor crash findings (April 7, 2026)
Musk said SpaceX would have about 3 gigawatts of computing power online by the end of this year and 13 gigawatts by the end of next year, with a “non-zero possibility” of exceeding 20 gigawatts. That capacity could position SpaceX to compete with major cloud computing providers, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Google.
Earlier this year, Musk had already merged his AI company, xAI, with SpaceX in a deal that valued SpaceX at $1 trillion and xAI at $250 billion.
In June, SpaceX priced its initial public offering at $135 per share, raising a record $75 billion through the sale of 555.56 million shares. The offering valued the company at $1.77 trillion, setting a record for a U.S. IPO.

Rockets, robots and risk: Elon Musk's US$3.6 trillion gamble to merge Tesla and SpaceX
Elon Musk Says Tesla, SpaceX Form Committees to Weigh Merger
sources.text:
Elon Musk says that Tesla and SpaceX have each set up special committees to discuss a possible merger between the two companies he leads as CEO.
The Wall Street Journal reports that Musk made the announcement on SpaceX’s quarterly earnings call, saying he is not part of either committee evaluating the combination. “The special committees have not reached an agreement of the terms of any transaction and there is no guarantee that they will but I do think there is a lot of merit in combining the companies,” he said.
Any deal would need a vote from shareholders of both companies. Tesla is valued at around $1.5 trillion and SpaceX at around $2 trillion. Musk holds substantial ownership stakes in both and has majority voting power at SpaceX.
Musk founded SpaceX in 2002 with proceeds from the sale of PayPal, which he co-founded. He joined Tesla’s board after investing in the company in 2004 and became its CEO in 2008. Folding SpaceX into Tesla would echo a pattern: Musk led the merger of his AI startup xAI into SpaceX earlier this year, and he was Tesla’s largest shareholder when it bought the struggling solar energy company SolarCity, which he was the largest shareholder of, in 2016.
SpaceX’s financial results, also released Tuesday, showed quarterly revenue of $14.6 billion, more than double what it reported a year earlier and ahead of analyst forecasts polled by FactSet. The company posted an overall profit of $4.4 billion for the quarter. Capital expenditures reached $19.6 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, and Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen said the company expects capital spending to nearly double again next quarter.
Musk opened the call, livestreamed on X, with a simulated video of an upcoming Starship launch set to classical music, calling it a “milestone in the history of civilization and consciousness.”
Much of the quarter’s growth came from the company’s AI business, which Musk recently renamed “SpaceX Super Intelligence.” Revenue from that segment surged nearly 830 percent to $7.6 billion, fueled by the February acquisition of xAI. The unit includes income from renting out data-center space to other AI companies, subscriptions to the Grok chatbot, and the GrokBot virtual assistant, which came through the $60 billion Cursor acquisition. Musk said SpaceX could be running about 13 gigawatts of computing power by the end of next year, with the potential to climb to 23 gigawatts. The company had 1.7 gigawatts in operation during the third quarter.
SpaceX’s traditional space business brought in $1.8 billion in revenue, up 6 percent from a year ago. Its connectivity business, which includes Starlink, reported $5.2 billion in revenue, up nearly 70 percent. Starlink’s consumer subscriber base grew to 13.6 million as of September 30, up from 12 million three months earlier. Executives pointed to newly acquired spectrum and said SpaceX wants to become a major U.S. mobile phone service provider.
Executives also addressed Starship, the roughly 400-foot rocket central to SpaceX’s future plans. They said the vehicle needs to fly regularly to support NASA lunar missions, bolster Starlink and eventually deploy AI data centers in space, something Musk said could happen as soon as 2027. In late September, SpaceX launched a Starship test flight that demonstrated the rocket’s ability to reach orbit. Musk said he expects the next test flight next month, which will include an attempt to catch the booster and upper stage for potential reuse.
Read more at the Wall Street Journal here.

sources.news_title: Elon Musk signals Tesla and SpaceX could merge. Here's why he thinks it's a good idea.
sources.text:
Elon Musk signals Tesla and SpaceX could merge. Here's why he thinks it's a good idea.
Elon Musk on Tuesday said SpaceX and Tesla are exploring a merger — a business combination that one Wall Street analyst said could be worth nearly $5 trillion, which would make it the largest deal in corporate history.
"Both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea at the request of shareholders, and these special committees consist of independent directors," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call with investors, adding that he sees "a lot of merit to combining the companies."
Tesla's stock price rose $14.01, or 3.8%, to $387.72, while SpaceX shares jumped $14.62, or 9.9%, to $162.41 in morning trading. Here's what to know about a possible merger between the companies.
How big would a SpaceX-Tesla merger be?
The merger would likely be valued at close to $5 trillion, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at investment firm Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News.
SpaceX is currently valued at $1.98 trillion, while Tesla's market capitalization stands at about $1.5 trillion. But Tesla shareholders would likely demand a premium for their shares to agree to the merger, Ives noted.
"For the merger to get passed by shareholders, it would have to be a higher price for Tesla — likely in the $500/$550 per share range in our view," he said.
That would make the combined company one of the most valuable in the world, rivaling that of the most highly valued businesses like chipmaker Nvidia, worth $5.2 trillion, or Apple, valued at $4.95 trillion.
What is the strategic rationale for merging the companies?
The main reason for combining SpaceX, a space exploration and AI company, with an electric vehicle manufacturer is to position them for a future in which artificial intelligence, or what Musk terms "super intelligence," becomes increasingly essential to everyday life.
"There's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing super intelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass to orbit with the Starmind constellation," Musk said in Tuesday's earnings call.
While Tesla's primary business remains manufacturing EVs, Musk has signaled that the company is shifting away from traditional motor vehicles. In January, the Tesla CEO said the company would phase out production of its Model S and Model X vehicles.
Instead, the company is changing course to focus on developing autonomous products, such as self-driving taxis and humanoid robots. Musk said Tesla will eventually produce 1 million humanoid robots a year as the company transitions to an "autonomous future." The humanoid robot, called Optimus, could hit the market in 2027, Musk said in January.
AI is essential to Optimus, allowing it to follow orders and take on various tasks, as well as to Tesla's push into self-driving robotaxis.
Meanwhile, SpaceX owns xAI, Musk's AI unit that created Grok, the chatbot that is used in the social media app X and other Musk-owned products. Musk's planned Terafab chip factory will tie all the businesses together by manufacturing semiconductors for both SpaceX and Tesla.
Combining the businesses makes sense for a "number of strategic AI and data-driven reasons, and this is the right move for Musk," Ives said in a research note.
What are the hurdles to a merger?
On Tuesday's conference call, Musk underlined that a merger of SpaceX and Tesla is far from assured, noting that a majority of Tesla shareholders would need to vote in favor of the combination.
"I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it," he said.
Musk added, "At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this, and particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50% vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that's quite a high hurdle to try to achieve."
Even so, Ives assigns an 80% to 90% chance that the merger will happen by the end of 2027.

sources.news_title: Wall St says Tesla-SpaceX deal inevitable but Musk says it’s not certain
sources.text: A Tesla-SpaceX merger appears to be a matter of when, not if, to many on Wall Street. But they disagree on a key factor: how much Tesla shareholders should be paid. That tension runs through a deal where predictions on the premium Tesla shareholders would get to swap into a stock of SpaceX that Elon Musk controls run from little or none to 35 per cent. With Tesla worth about US$1.5 trillion, the premium could run into hundreds of billions of dollars, making it a major swing factor in any deal. The billionaire, a self-described ‘conflicted party’, said the committees are yet to agree on terms, even as Wall Street sees a deal being proposed in the coming months. Tesla shares gained more than three per cent, while SpaceX rose 11 per cent on Wednesday and was set to add about US$210 billion to its market capitalization if gains hold, roughly equal to that of CitiGroup. SpaceX and Tesla are jointly developing the Terafab chip plant, and AI now makes up more than half of SpaceX’s revenue, with another US$35 billion to US$40 billion spending likely in fourth quarter to fund further expansion. “(A Tesla-SpaceX merger) is very strategic as both companies are rapidly transitioning into artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, and both have huge infrastructure projects underway,” said Justus Parmar, CEO of Fortuna Investments and an investor in both companies. “It would also avoid redundancy and the time he spends going back and forth between two entities, and there would be a reduction in public company overhead, legal costs and administrative burdens.” Analysts have said that burgeoning capital spending for expensive AI and space infrastructure would weigh on SpaceX’s free cash flow, a strain a combined company could ease by sharing services and borrowing jointly with Tesla. They also pointed to last week’s Roadster unveiling, where a Tesla car built with SpaceX rocket thrusters flipped and leapt over vehicles, as a teaser for what a combined company could produce. However, much of the technology on which the lofty valuations of the companies are based, including data centers in orbit, self-driving taxis at scale and humanoid robots, has yet to reach commercial scale. That would take years of heavy spending and engineering, adding execution risk to a deal already facing questions over governance and price. “The big reason why this makes so much sense is that what Tesla is doing SpaceX needs and what SpaceX is doing Tesla needs,” Gene Munster, managing partner at Tesla investor Deepwater Asset Management, said on X. “And both of them operate under the grand vision which is Elon building a true vertical AI company.” Premium: the next battle Price is likely to be the next fight. Tesla shareholders would be swapping a stake in an independent company, where Musk holds about 20 per cent of the vote, for shares in SpaceX that Musk controls. RBC Capital Markets and JPMorgan analysts expect investors would want a premium of between 20 per cent and 35 per cent, but some do not expect a premium. Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki, whose firm owns both stocks, argues that any premium would dilute SpaceX shareholders as its spending bills rise. Michael Monaghan of Founder ETFs said the overlap between the two shareholder bases means he does not expect a substantial premium. Tesla vote is the hurdle Control may also be part of Musk’s appeal for a merger. Musk holds about 85 per cent of SpaceX’s voting power through super-voting shares. But at Tesla he has roughly 20 per cent. Bill Birmingham, head of research at REX Financial, estimates a merger would give the billionaire about 57 per cent of voting rights. Ryan Zurrer, founder of Dialectic, puts it at 58 per cent at an exchange ratio of 0.7 of one SpaceX share, the illustrative level Barclays has floated. No ratio has been negotiated. Zurrer said a ratio near 0.6 would be needed for Musk to keep control if he sold more equity, and that “the biggest hurdle will be the Tesla shareholders vote vs Elon’s own incentives.” Musk said Tesla side needs a majority of all shares, not just those voted, so every uncast ballot counts against a deal. Analysts have flagged turnout as a risk, citing uncast broker votes at last year’s meeting as a potential factor that could affect chances of a deal going through. Governance and regulatory questions would follow. When Tesla bought SolarCity in 2016, a Delaware court cleared it after years of litigation but said it should have formed an independent committee. “A deal where one man runs both sides will draw tough questions on governance,” said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at eToro. Tesla is set to report third-quarter results after markets close. Analysts said they were also watching out for disclosures of merger talks in regulatory filings ahead of the automaker’s Dec. 3 annual shareholder meeting. --- Reporting by Abhirup Roy in San Francisco and Akash Sriram in Bengaluru; Additional reporting by Arpan Daniel Varghese in Bengaluru; Editing by Arun Koyyur

sources.news_title: SpaceX and Tesla Form Merger Exploration Committee That Excludes Elon Musk
sources.text:
The possible marriage of Tesla (TSLA +3.41%) and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +7.80%) is getting serious attention now that Elon Musk, CEO of both companies, has confirmed that each has formed committees of independent directors to explore a potential merger.
Musk isn't participating in the discussions because his ownership interests in both companies create a conflict of interest. And while he cautioned a merger isn't guaranteed, the logic behind combining these two mammoth companies is difficult to ignore.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
Why a Tesla-SpaceX merger makes sense
Tesla got its start as an electric vehicle company and played a significant role in bringing EVs to the mainstream. Musk and Tesla proved that EVs didn't have to be underpowered -- Tesla built cars that perform well and look good.
But Tesla has been moving beyond EVs, with Musk's ambitions now including autonomous robotaxis, the Optimus humanoid robot, and artificial intelligence systems capable of operating in the physical world. Tesla shuttered production lines for two of its early EVs, the Model S and Model X, to free up factory space to manufacture its Optimus robot line.
SpaceX, which went public in June with the largest IPO in history, encompasses satellite communications, rocket launch capabilities, and AI computing infrastructure. It's long been seen as a potential merger partner for Tesla, with analyst Dan Ives predicting less than a week after SpaceX's IPO that the two companies would merge within a year.
A combined Tesla-SpaceX could develop AI models, provide the computing infrastructure to train them, and deploy that intelligence through vehicles, robots, and potentially spacecraft.
There are already examples of the two companies working together. Tesla recently unveiled a second-generation Roadster that featured a flashy model incorporating SpaceX technology, giving it limited flight capabilities (the flying Roadster won't be for sale to the public).

But sharing technology across separate companies isn't necessarily the most efficient arrangement. A merger could allow the businesses to coordinate research, infrastructure investments, and capital allocation under one corporate structure.
It would also bring Musk's increasingly interconnected business ambitions under one roof.
SpaceX's earnings make a compelling merger case
The merger disclosure came alongside an outstanding quarter for SpaceX, which reported revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161% from a year earlier. Net income reached $4.4 billion, reversing a $1.1 billion loss in the third quarter of 2025.
But the most interesting development wasn't in its rocket business. SpaceX's AI business (which it now calls SI, or Super Intelligence) generated $7.6 billion in revenue, making artificial intelligence its largest business by sales. Meanwhile, its connectivity segment, which includes Starlink, produced $5.2 billion.
SpaceX is also investing heavily in expanding its AI infrastructure, with capital expenditures reaching $19.6 billion during the quarter. That investment creates opportunities for collaboration with Tesla, which has its own enormous computing requirements.
Here's the biggest obstacle to a SpaceX-Tesla merger
There's a substantial difference between a merger making strategic sense and shareholders getting a good deal.
SpaceX's aggressive investment in AI infrastructure requires enormous amounts of capital, and Tesla shareholders could find themselves helping finance projects that have little immediate connection to selling vehicles or developing autonomous driving technology.
Then there's the question of valuation. Both companies have attracted investors willing to pay substantial premiums for their future growth prospects. Combining them doesn't automatically justify those expectations.
Any transaction would also require agreement between the independent committees and possibly shareholder approval. Musk's enthusiasm alone won't get it done. Still, the formation of these committees suggests the merger discussion has advanced beyond Wall Street speculation. And Tesla shareholders have been willing to follow Musk, even accepting his demands last year for a 10-year compensation package worth up to $1 trillion.
Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly pursuing different parts of the same technological ambitions. Keeping them separate may eventually become harder to justify than combining them.
For now, Musk is trying to downplay the possibility. "Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty," he said. "I think that would be overstating it."
But the business rationale for a merger is getting stronger, and investors now have concrete evidence that both companies are exploring the possibility.

NEW YORK (AP) — SpaceX reported a bigger quarterly profit than expected Tuesday as its satellite communications and artificial intelligence businesses boomed.
The company, run by Elon Musk, posted a profit for the three months through September of $4.4 billion, or 35 cents per share, reversing a year-ago loss and easily topping Wall Street’s expectations. Revenue soared to $14.6 billion, up 161%.
On a conference call with analysts, Musk suggested a merger with his electric car company Tesla might be in the works, something that has been rumored for months. He said both companies formed “special committees” of independent directors to discuss the issue, though he played down the chances of an imminent deal.
“Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty,” he said. “I think that would be overstating it.”
The AI business became SpaceX’s largest by revenue in the third quarter, although the Starlink satellite service remains the biggest profit generator.
“They beat across all metrics and the Starlink business looks to be accelerating,” said Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives. “This is just what (Wall) Street wanted.”
The stock rose 7.5% in after-hours trading.
Musk also told analysts that for next month’s launch of its Starship rocket, SpaceX will attempt to grab both the booster and ship with mechanical arms upon return to base, a key step toward demonstrating it can reuse the massive spacecraft.
“The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle,” Musk said, calling the attempt, if successful, “a massive technology milestone.”
SpaceX hopes to get Starship on a regular launch pattern in preparation for NASA’s upcoming lunar missions.
The company already has huge contracts with the federal government, and House Democrats have called for investigations into those contracts and Musk’s work with the Department of Government Efficiency. Musk has spent $276 million since July in support of Republican candidates.

Tesla and SpaceX Just Formed Special Committees to Weigh a Merger
Elon Musk confirmed on SpaceX's earnings call that both companies formed special committees to explore a deal he cannot personally join. What shareholders decide next could reshape a combined company worth over three trillion dollars.
Elon Musk used SpaceX’s (NASDAQ:SPCX | SPCX Price Prediction) third-quarter earnings call on October 20, 2026, to disclose something neither company had put in writing. When an analyst asked about a tie-up, Musk said, “Both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea at the request of shareholders.”
He said the committees are made up of independent directors. Because he runs both companies, he is a conflicted party and cannot take part in their discussions.
Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) closed at $373.71, up 1.54%, and traded at $380.29 after hours. SpaceX closed at $147.79 and moved to $159.70 after its quarterly report, a gain of 8.06%.
For Tesla owners, a merger could fold a low-margin car business into a faster-growing company. But Tesla stock is down 16.9% this year, and no price or terms have been disclosed.
What Musk Said and What He Left Out
Musk said assuming a merger is a certainty “would be overstating it” and added, “the special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transaction. And obviously, there’s no guarantee that they will.”
He still argued for the deal: “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the super intelligence singularity.” He called the process “an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can’t be in the conversation.”
A Tesla Vote Is the Hardest Step
Elon Musk said Tesla would need “a 50% vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders,” and called that “quite a high hurdle to try to achieve.” Under that standard, every share that never votes works like a no vote. Tesla has a large retail base, and many small holders ignore proxy ballots.
Tesla’s proxy, filed October 19, sets the annual meeting for December 3, 2026, and lists three company proposals. None of them is a merger vote, so any deal would go to shareholders at a later meeting.
The two companies are already tied together.
On January 16, 2026, Tesla agreed to invest about $2.00 billion in xAI Holdings Series E preferred stock. xAI Holdings became a SpaceX subsidiary on February 2, 2026, and Tesla director Ira Ehrenpreis has served on SpaceX’s board since then.
Musk runs both companies and controls SpaceX’s voting power, so he sits on both sides of any price. That conflict is the reason independent committees are needed.
At the October 20 close, Tesla was worth $1.48 trillion, and SpaceX was worth $2.01 trillion. If the two combined, Tesla holders would own less than half of the new company.
The exchange ratio, meaning how many SpaceX shares each Tesla share would turn into, is the central unknown, and nothing about it has been disclosed. Gene Munster put the chance of a combination within two years at 95%. That is one investor’s estimate, and Musk himself was more cautious.
Why Tesla’s Standalone Numbers Matter Before Any Deal
On its own business, Tesla is hard to justify at 389 times earnings. Second-quarter non-GAAP EPS of $0.33 missed the $0.5367 estimate, operating margin fell to 1.4%, and free cash flow was -$1.092 billion.
Third-quarter deliveries of 486,532 show that demand is holding up, but profits have not kept pace. The merger option does not change that, because the ratio is unknown and the vote threshold is high.
SpaceX holders would be the larger side of any deal. SpaceX’s quarter brought $4.40 billion in GAAP net income.
Tesla reports after the close on October 21 and holds a webcast at 5:30 p.m. ET. The next signal to look for is a filing, because talk becomes a real process only if either company files an 8-K that names committee members, advisors, or terms.

Adjusted EBITDA, a company-defined non-GAAP measure that excludes depreciation, amortization and share-based compensation, among other items, rose 306% to $8.81 billion.

SI reported $431 million in operating income, including $1.2 billion in share-based compensation expense linked to the Cursor acquisition. sources.news_title: Musk steps back as SpaceX and Tesla explore potentially historic deal
sources.text:
Elon Musk has spent years building companies that appear to belong to different industries. Now, as artificial intelligence begins to reshape the economics of his business empire, the world’s richest person is considering whether he should make it one.
Musk said on Tuesday that combining SpaceX and Tesla would be “a good idea”, confirming for the first time that the two companies had established special committees to discuss a possible merger. The announcement sent SpaceX shares up 8 per cent in extended trading, while Tesla gained 1.8 per cent.
The prospect of a union would bring together an electric vehicle manufacturer struggling to define its next phase of growth with a space and satellite business increasingly powered by artificial intelligence. It could also consolidate Musk’s control over an extraordinary range of technologies, from autonomous machines and semiconductor manufacturing to global communications and computing infrastructure in orbit.
But Musk cautioned investors against treating a deal as inevitable. The independent committees had yet to agree on terms, he said, and might never reach an agreement.
“I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” Musk told investors on a conference call. He added that he was a “conflicted party” and could not participate in their discussions.
The committees were established at shareholders’ request, Musk said, meaning any eventual transaction would face scrutiny from investors whose interests may not necessarily align with his own.
Musk owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and just under half of SpaceX. A merger could give him control of a combined business that reaches from the factory floor to low-Earth orbit.
The AI engine changes everything
The discussions come as SpaceX undergoes a dramatic financial transformation.
The company reported revenue of $14.58bn for the three months to September 30, up 161 per cent from a year earlier. Net income reached $4.4bn, compared with a loss of $1.1bn in the same period last year, comfortably exceeding analysts’ expectations.
The most striking development was artificial intelligence. Revenue from the business surged almost tenfold to $7.56bn, largely driven by renting data-centre computing capacity to developers including Anthropic, Google and Reflection AI.
Musk told investors he expected annual recurring revenue of between $500bn and $1tn by the end of 2027, reflecting his confidence in the extraordinary growth potential of AI infrastructure.
The scale of that ambition comes with a formidable price tag. Capital expenditure nearly tripled to $19.6bn in the third quarter, while chief financial officer Bret Johnsen said spending could reach $35bn-$40bn in the fourth quarter.
“SpaceX delivered the quarter the bulls wanted, at least on the top line,” said Will Rhind, chief executive of asset manager GraniteShares. “The story now is all about AI.”
The figures suggest SpaceX is becoming something more complex than a rocket company. Its financial engine increasingly resembles that of a cloud-computing provider, while its longer-term plans depend on Starship becoming a reliable, reusable vehicle capable of carrying infrastructure into orbit.
One empire, multiple frontiers
Musk argues that combining SpaceX and Tesla could accelerate development across several overlapping technologies.
He pointed to “superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity”.
Terafab, the proposed chip-manufacturing venture between the companies, is expected to produce its first test chip around May or June next year, with volume production targeted for the third quarter of 2028.
The strategic logic is clear enough. Tesla’s ambitions in robotics and autonomous driving require computing power and advanced chips. SpaceX offers satellite connectivity, launch capacity and a potential route towards orbital computing infrastructure. A combined organisation could coordinate investment across those fields rather than negotiate arrangements between separate companies.
Yet the breadth of the vision is also a source of risk. Integrating businesses with different capital requirements, regulatory obligations and shareholder constituencies could prove considerably harder than presenting them as complementary parts of a technological revolution.
A person familiar with the discussions told Reuters that talks had begun in recent weeks and could result in SpaceX acquiring Tesla. The person said Tesla had been working with an investment bank on the discussions.
No transaction terms have been agreed, and the direction of any deal remains uncertain.
SpaceX’s core satellite business provides a substantial foundation. Starlink had 13.6mn subscribers in the third quarter, exceeding analysts’ expectations of 12.19mn, supported by expansion into consumer, aviation, maritime, enterprise and government markets.
But growth has involved trade-offs. Average monthly revenue per subscriber has fallen from $99 in 2023 to $69 in the latest quarter as the company expands into markets where customers pay less.
Meanwhile, Starship has yet to enter commercial service. Its eventual success is central to plans for deploying more powerful Starlink satellites and establishing computing infrastructure in space, but development remains expensive and technically demanding.
For Tesla shareholders, a merger could provide access to a broader technological platform. It could equally expose them to greater capital demands and a business whose priorities extend far beyond selling vehicles.
The central question is whether the proposed union would unlock efficiencies unavailable to two separate companies — or concentrate too much financial and strategic risk in a single corporate structure.
Musk has built his career on persuading investors to finance technologies whose commercial potential initially seemed improbable. His latest proposition is more ambitious still: that cars, robots, chips, satellites and artificial intelligence should be treated not as separate markets, but as components of one integrated system.
SpaceX’s latest results suggest the money is beginning to follow that vision. Whether shareholders will agree to combine the empire behind it remains the next, and potentially decisive, test.

sources.news_title: Why Does Elon Musk Want to Merge SpaceX and Tesla Into a $3.5 Trillion Empire?
sources.text:
Elon Musk has publicly backed the idea of merging Tesla and SpaceX, a move that could create a technology giant valued at approximately $3.5 trillion and bring electric vehicles, rockets, satellite communications, artificial intelligence and robotics under one corporate structure.
Musk said on Tuesday that combining the companies had considerable merit as he expands his ambitions beyond electric vehicles and space launches into advanced computing, autonomous systems and potentially orbital data centres.
The two businesses were once viewed as largely separate ventures. Tesla built its reputation on electric vehicles and battery storage, while SpaceX focused on rockets, satellite internet and space transportation. Their activities are increasingly converging, however, as Musk pursues an integrated technology ecosystem spanning manufacturing, energy, communications and AI.
A merger could give that vision a more unified corporate structure. But it would also expose investors to complex regulatory, geopolitical and financial risks.
Stay ahead of the geopolitical week.
MD Briefing delivers expert analysis across five global fronts — the Indo-Pacific, energy, geoeconomics, European security, and the Middle East — every Monday morning. Free.
Why Does Musk Want to Combine Tesla and SpaceX?
Musk’s central argument is that the companies could achieve more by coordinating their resources rather than operating independently.
He has identified potential cooperation in AI software, semiconductor design, robotics, satellite connectivity and the development of computing infrastructure in space. These projects increasingly depend on overlapping technologies, from advanced chips and energy systems to automated manufacturing and high-speed communications.
A merger could also simplify decision-making. Musk’s long-term projects often involve multiple companies, each with its own boards, shareholders and capital requirements. Bringing Tesla and SpaceX together could make it easier to direct engineering talent, investment and infrastructure towards shared priorities.
Control is another consideration. Musk owns nearly one-fifth of Tesla and has voting control at SpaceX. A merger could consolidate his influence over a wider range of businesses and give management greater flexibility to pursue projects that cross traditional industry boundaries.
However, the strategic logic depends on whether these businesses can generate meaningful benefits from working together. Combining corporate structures does not automatically make expensive research programmes more efficient or ensure that ambitious technologies become commercially viable.
What Would a Merger Mean for Investors?
A combined company could give investors exposure to a much broader portfolio of businesses.
Tesla shareholders would gain access to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite broadband operation, rocket launch services and future space ventures. SpaceX investors, in turn, would gain exposure to Tesla’s electric vehicles, battery storage, autonomous driving and robotics operations.
The resulting business could command a valuation of around $3.5 trillion, according to the proposed combination’s estimated value. That would place it among the world’s most valuable corporations, although such a valuation would depend on the transaction’s terms and how investors assess the combined assets.
Supporters could argue that a single corporate structure would allow more efficient allocation of capital across interconnected technologies. For example, investments in chips, batteries and AI computing could potentially serve several business divisions instead of being developed separately.
The risks, however, would also become more interconnected. Investors would be exposed to the performance of electric vehicles, commercial spaceflight, satellite services, autonomous technology and robotics simultaneously.
These businesses have different revenue models, investment cycles and regulatory requirements. A setback in one major project could affect the wider company, while disagreements over capital allocation could create tensions between investors with different priorities.
Where Could Tesla and SpaceX Work Together?
The strongest argument for a merger lies in the potential links between their technologies and infrastructure.
Artificial intelligence and semiconductor production
Musk has announced Terafab, a semiconductor and AI-computing project intended to produce advanced chips for Tesla’s autonomous vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots, as well as SpaceX’s AI and data-centre ambitions. He hopes the project can begin volume production by late 2028.
A combined company could coordinate chip development and computing investment across its different operations. Yet semiconductor manufacturing is capital-intensive and technically demanding, and the proposed production timeline remains an ambition rather than a guaranteed outcome.
Satellite communications and autonomous systems
SpaceX’s Starlink network could potentially support communications for Tesla’s robotaxis, autonomous systems and future generations of humanoid robots. Reliable connectivity could become increasingly important as autonomous technologies expand across different environments.
The extent of these benefits would depend on technical requirements, network capacity, regulatory approvals and the commercial arrangements governing the services.
Energy and data centres
Tesla’s battery and energy-storage technologies could help support the electricity requirements of AI computing facilities and future data-centre projects associated with SpaceX. As AI infrastructure expands, access to reliable power and efficient storage is becoming an increasingly important business consideration.
Musk has also discussed the possibility of placing data centres in orbit. Such infrastructure could eventually form part of a wider space-based computing strategy, although substantial technical, financial and operational challenges remain.
Manufacturing and supply chains
Tesla’s experience in large-scale factory automation could complement SpaceX’s efforts to increase the production of rockets and other space hardware. The companies could also coordinate procurement of electronics, specialised materials, batteries and manufacturing equipment.
These potential synergies provide a rationale for closer cooperation. The unresolved question is whether a full merger would deliver greater benefits than commercial partnerships and shared projects between two separate companies.
Could Geopolitics Derail the Deal?
Regulatory and national-security concerns could prove among the most difficult obstacles to combining the businesses.
SpaceX is a major contractor for the US military, intelligence agencies and NASA. Its work involves sensitive technologies and strategic infrastructure, making ownership, governance and access to information important considerations for US authorities.
Tesla, meanwhile, has substantial exposure to China through its Shanghai factory, which plays a major role in its manufacturing operations and sales. Combining a strategically significant US space contractor with a company deeply connected to the Chinese market could attract heightened scrutiny from American regulators and national-security officials, as well as attention from Beijing.
The merger would also raise questions about corporate governance. Investors would need to assess how the transaction values each business, whether the terms fairly compensate shareholders and how Musk’s voting power would affect oversight.
Potential conflicts of interest could become particularly important because Musk already exercises significant influence across several companies. Shareholders would need confidence that decisions about investment, technology transfers and the allocation of resources serve the interests of the combined business.
Would a Merger Make Musk’s Vision More Achievable?
Combining Tesla and SpaceX could create a powerful platform for Musk’s ambitions in AI, robotics, energy, satellite communications and space infrastructure. It could also make it easier to coordinate projects that increasingly depend on common technologies and manufacturing capabilities.
But a larger corporate structure would not eliminate the risks surrounding these ventures. Starship development, robotaxis, humanoid robots, advanced semiconductor production and orbital data centres all require substantial investment and face significant technical challenges.
The merger would therefore represent more than a corporate restructuring. It would be a test of whether one company can manage an unusually diverse portfolio of technologies while satisfying shareholders, regulators and national-security authorities.
Ultimately, the key question is not simply whether Tesla and SpaceX can be combined, but whether bringing them under one roof would create more value than allowing each business to focus on its own priorities. For Musk, the potential reward is an integrated technology empire. For investors, the challenge will be determining whether that ambition justifies the financial and strategic risks.
With information from Reuters.

sources.news_title: SPACEX POSTS A PROFIT, AND MUSK HINTS AT A TESLA MERGER
sources.text:
SpaceX reported a quarterly profit that came in above expectations, driven by growth in its satellite communications operations and its business of leasing computing power to other companies, and Elon Musk used the moment to openly endorse the prospect of combining SpaceX with Tesla in what would be the biggest corporate merger on record.
The Washington Times summarized the turn on Tuesday morning: "SpaceX turns a profit after a string of losses as its satellite and computer leasing businesses soar." The report followed a company disclosure that net income for the three months through September reached four point four billion dollars, or thirty-five cents per share — more than double the figure from the comparable period a year earlier, according to WRAL.com.
Bloomberg reported that the profit "surges past estimates on AI and satellite internet growth," and that Musk "openly endorsed the prospect of combining SpaceX with Tesla Inc., in what would be the biggest-ever corporate merger uniting assets from electric cars to AI data centers to rocket and satellite capabilities."
WRAL.com described the same quarter as one in which "satellite communications and artificial intelligence businesses boomed," and noted the company is run by Musk. The earnings figure, the per-share result and the year-over-year comparison all come from that account of the filing.
What traveled fastest was not the balance sheet but the merger remark. The suggestion that Tesla and SpaceX could be folded into a single entity set off a round of commentary that treated the earnings report as a prelude rather than the story itself. The Washington Times framed the quarter around the operating businesses; Bloomberg framed it around both the profit and Musk's stated openness to a combination; WRAL framed it around the scale of the earnings beat. Each of those framings was picked up and argued over separately.
The profit itself is the concrete claim in the reporting: net income of four point four billion dollars for the September quarter, thirty-five cents per share, more than double the prior-year figure, on the strength of satellite communications and leased computing capacity. The merger talk is described as Musk's endorsement of the prospect — a statement of openness, not an announced transaction.
The distinction matters because the reaction frequently blurred the two. A quarterly profit is a filed number. A merger between Tesla and SpaceX would require corporate action that nobody in the reporting describes as underway or scheduled. Bloomberg's language is that Musk "openly endorsed the prospect" — the prospect, not the deal.
Next News Network could not independently verify the reported figures or the merger remarks.
The background is a company that had posted a string of losses before this quarter. That history is the reason the profit drew notice at all: SpaceX spent years as a capital-intensive launch business whose financial results were measured against its ability to fund development rather than against earnings. The satellite communications side — the Starlink constellation — and the newer business of leasing computing capacity to outside companies are what the reporting credits with the swing.
Those two lines of business are also what connect the earnings story to the merger talk. A rocket company that also sells broadband and rents out computing power sits alongside an electric vehicle manufacturer that has moved into AI data centers. Bloomberg's description of a combined company — "from electric cars to AI data centers to rocket and satellite capabilities" — is essentially a list of the assets the two firms already hold.
The reactions divided along predictable lines. Some commentators treated the profit as vindication of a long, expensive build-out and pointed to the leased computing business as evidence the company had found a second revenue engine beyond launch services. Others treated the merger remark as the more consequential item, arguing that combining the two companies would concentrate an unusual range of infrastructure — launch, broadband, vehicles and data centers — under one roof, and said so plainly.
The earnings beat also drew the attention of commentators who had spent years predicting the satellite business would not pay for itself. The reported profit gave those arguments a concrete number to work against, and the number was large enough that the terms of the debate shifted from whether the business could be profitable to how durable the profitability would prove.
None of that settles the merger question. An endorsement of a prospect is not a filing, and the reporting describes no transaction, no timetable and no structure. The earnings figures are the company's own, as relayed by the outlets covering them, and the merger remark is Musk's, as characterized by Bloomberg.
What the sequence shows is how quickly a quarterly result becomes a platform for a much larger argument. The profit was the news on Tuesday morning. By the time the coverage circulated, the conversation had moved to what the profit might make possible — and to whether one person should control that much of it.
Our Take
The left has spent years telling anyone who would listen that Starlink was a money pit and that Musk's space venture would never stop burning cash. Tuesday's numbers make that argument harder to repeat with a straight face: four point four billion dollars in net income in a single quarter is not a rounding error, and it came from exactly the two businesses the skeptics said would never scale — satellite broadband and leased computing capacity. When the critics pivot from "it will never be profitable" to "the merger is scary," that is the sound of an argument being abandoned in real time.
Note what the reaction actually reveals. The same commentators who demand that corporations be transparent about their finances went quiet on the earnings and loud on the merger hint, because the earnings undercut a narrative and the merger hint feeds one. If Tesla and SpaceX combine, it would be the largest corporate merger ever — and it would also be a voluntary transaction between a company and its shareholders, subject to the same disclosure and approval rules as any other. The people warning about concentration of power in one man's hands are the same people who cheered when the federal government leaned on social media platforms to police speech. Their concern about concentrated authority is selective, and everyone can see it.
And the fusion of electric vehicles, AI data centers, rockets and satellite broadband is precisely the kind of integrated industrial capability this country needs to compete with China. Beijing is not waiting for permission to build national champions. If Washington's instinct is to smother an American company for growing too capable, the next generation of launch and communications infrastructure will be built somewhere else by someone who does not have to answer to a Senate hearing. The profit is the proof the model works. The merger talk is a signal about what comes next — and the reaction tells you who is afraid of it.

Musk argued that combining the companies would allow them to deepen cooperation on chip design, robotics, software, and other technologies; both firms’ share prices rose following the announcement.
In this article:
Liz’s view
The outlines of MegaMusk Inc. are starting to emerge, where special committees of SpaceX and Tesla directors will now have to bless the merger. Combining the two would bring the tech and infrastructure parts of Musk’s empire together (the Wall Street pitch) and a hyperconcentrated bet on the billionaire’s inventions, politics, and personality (the actual pitch).

sources.news_title: Why Elon Musk Wants to Merge SpaceX and Tesla
sources.text:
The world’s richest man has publicly backed a potential combination of SpaceX and Tesla in what could be the biggest merger in history.
On Tuesday, Elon Musk, the CEO and largest shareholder of both companies, said the electric vehicle maker and the rocket company had formed special committees at the request of shareholders to discuss the idea.
“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating,” Musk told SpaceX investors on a conference call.
“I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” he added.
The committees, which are made up of independent directors, would need to agree on the transaction terms of any deal before putting it to shareholders for a vote. Musk said his conflict of interest prevents him from participating in their discussions.
Musk has previously teased a Tesla-SpaceX merger. On a July 22 earnings call, Musk said there was “more and more overlap” between Tesla and SpaceX as the companies expand into artificial intelligence and robotics. Last week, Barclays analysts suggested that a merger could be announced before Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting in December.
Tuesday’s call was the first confirmation that the companies were formally exploring a combination.
A merger could create a company worth around $3.5 trillion, putting it among the world’s most valuable companies. It could also become the biggest merger ever by deal value, potentially surpassing SpaceX’s record-setting $250 billion acquisition of Musk-owned AI company xAI in February. SpaceX is currently valued at about $2 trillion, and Tesla at $1.5 trillion. A deal could also help propel Musk back into trillionaire ranks, depending on its terms and how investors value the combined company. Musk owns around 48% of SpaceX and 20% of Tesla.
The shares of both companies rose in after-hours trading on Tuesday. SpaceX, which went public in June, reported a quarterly net profit of $4.4 billion. Musk told investors he expects annual recurring revenue of between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027.
Some analysts, however, have warned of regulatory and geopolitical hurdles, particularly in terms of Tesla’s Chinese operations and SpaceX’s U.S. defence work. Morningstar analysts said a merger could raise U.S. national security concerns involving the combined company’s supply chain. JPMorgan analysts also flagged regulatory approval in China as a potential stumbling block.
Any deal could also face congressional scrutiny, which could intensify if Democrats win control of either chamber in the coming midterm elections. Democratic lawmakers have previously questioned Musk over conflicts of interest and raised national security concerns about reported Chinese investments in SpaceX. Democrats have also challenged major acquisitions in the past on consumer protection grounds. In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D, Mass.) criticized SpaceX’s IPO, citing Musk’s concentrated voting power and weak investor protections—concerns that could resurface in a Tesla-SpaceX merger.
Why a merger matters
A merger could bring two of Musk’s biggest businesses under one corporate umbrella, making it easier for the companies to move investments and resources between projects. “This would allow him to run all their operations under one roof without tripping on as many governance issues,” wrote Morningstar analysts Seth Goldstein and Nicolas Owens in June. “For example, Musk could move Tesla software developers or engineers to work on SpaceX AI projects, and vice versa, or have Tesla and SpaceX supply one another without the need for related party transaction disclosures or risking shareholder lawsuits claiming the resources of one firm are being diverted for the benefit of the other.”
Analysts noted that Tesla’s robotaxis could benefit from Starlink connectivity, while its autonomous vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots could more closely integrate SpaceX’s AI technology. SpaceX’s planned orbital data centers, meanwhile, could potentially benefit from access to Tesla’s battery and energy storage products.
A combined company could also mean greater control of several stages of the AI value chain, from chip design and planned manufacturing to computing infrastructure, AI software, and its deployment in vehicles and robots.
The companies already collaborate. In March, they announced Terafab, a joint semiconductor manufacturing project intended to produce chips for Tesla’s vehicles and humanoid robots and SpaceX’s planned AI satellites. SpaceX technologies have also been used in some Tesla products, including the new Roadster prototype, which uses SpaceX-developed thrusters.
David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group, told the BBC that a merger also appears to align with Musk’s long-held ambition of colonizing Mars. Musk previously outlined plans to send Tesla’s Optimus robots to the planet aboard SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft.
A merger could also strengthen Musk’s influence over Tesla’s direction. Barclays estimated that a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla could give Musk around 37% of the combined company while controlling around 56% of its voting power. He currently controls around 82% of voting power at SpaceX and 20% at Tesla. That could represent either a benefit or a risk for shareholders, as decision-making would become faster but have fewer checks.
“One thing I don’t think people talk enough about with SpaceX and Tesla as well: You do still have a huge amount of key-man risk here,” wrote Morningstar analyst David Sekera earlier this month. “God forbid anything were to happen to Elon Musk.”

Musk Says Tesla and SpaceX Have Merger Committees, but a Deal Is Far From Certain
Independent directors will examine the proposal as Musk recuses himself from discussions because of his interests in both companies
Elon Musk said on Tuesday that Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees of independent directors to explore a potential merger, but the billionaire repeatedly cautioned no transaction had been done yet.
During SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call, Musk said he supported the potential merger but could not participate in the special committees' discussions because he was a conflicted party.
A merger would unite two corporate giants, with SpaceX reportedly valued at around $2 trillion and Tesla at $1.5 trillion. However, these numbers are not finalised deal prices, and an official merger agreement has not yet been signed.
Navigating the Conflict of Interest
As chief executive officer of both companies and a significant shareholder, Musk has financial interests in each business. He said he was excluded from the exploratory discussions because of the conflict of interest, leaving the independent committees to examine the potential transaction.
Musk commented on the situation, describing it as an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and he cannot be in the conversation. He also described commenting on the prospective deal as tap dancing through a minefield.
The independent committees are intended to provide oversight of a potential transaction involving a significant conflict of interest. Their formation does not automatically eliminate fiduciary duties or potential legal liability, and the fairness of any eventual deal would depend on its terms and the process followed.
Wall Street Weighs in on the Pros and Cons
Analysts are currently divided on whether a merger would serve the shareholders. The companies' overlapping ambitions in artificial intelligence and chip development could provide a strategic rationale for a merger.
No transaction timeline has been confirmed. Reuters reported that Barclays had suggested a deal could be announced before Tesla's annual meeting in December, but the committees have not agreed on transaction terms.
Any proposed merger would require the companies to determine an appropriate valuation and exchange ratio. The terms would influence how much of the combined business Tesla shareholders would own, making the valuation process central to assessing whether a deal would benefit both shareholder groups.
The proposal could also raise concerns about valuation, profitability and capital allocation. Tesla shareholders would need to assess whether a combined business justified the price of the transaction and whether its investment commitments could affect returns.
A merger may also raise concerns about shareholder dilution and the allocation of capital between the companies' businesses. Investors would need to assess whether the transaction could affect Tesla's ability to fund priorities such as its Cybercab programme and Optimus humanoid robots.
The extent of any impact would depend on the final deal structure and financing arrangements.
The Stiff Hurdle of Shareholder Approval
Despite the strategic arguments, the path to a formalised transaction faces complex administrative and legal challenges. Musk has pointed out that the special committees have no guarantee of finding mutually agreeable terms.
Even if the independent committees agree on terms, securing shareholder approval remains a major obstacle. Musk noted that Tesla requires a vote from the majority of all outstanding shares, not just a simple majority of those present at the meeting.
This strict requirement should not be confused with a 'majority of the minority' vote, which typically protects unaffiliated shareholders from a controlling investor.
Without this necessary shareholder backing, the merger cannot go through on these terms, leaving the ultimate outcome dependent on legal thresholds, final agreements, and closing conditions.

sources.news_title: Musk mulls SpaceX-Tesla merger as companies form deal committees
sources.text:
Elon Musk opened talks of a potential merger of his two companies, SpaceX and Tesla, suggesting it would be "a good idea" and that they had formed special committees to discuss a union, sending shares of the space and technology company up 8% in extended trading.
SpaceX earlier posted its first profit as a public company, and Musk said he expected annual recurring revenue of between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027, as demand for its data-center space surges thanks to the AI boom.
Musk has in the past tantalized shareholders with the idea of combining SpaceX and Tesla, citing growing overlap between them. Speculation about the space company buying the EV maker has gained traction recently, with Barclays suggesting last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla's annual meeting in December.
"I think it would be a good idea, but it's really up to the special committees of both companies," Musk said in the first official confirmation that the companies were formally talking.
"Because I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions of the special committees," which comprised independent directors, he told investors on a conference call.
The companies had formed the special committees at the request of shareholders, who ultimately would need to approve a deal, he added.
"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity," he said.
Terafab, the chip manufacturing joint venture between the two companies, should produce its first test chip around May or June of next year and aims to reach volume production by the third quarter of 2028, Musk said on the call.
Musk added that it would be premature to assume a SpaceX-Tesla merger would happen, noting that the special committees had not agreed on transaction terms and may never do so. Tesla shares rose 1.8% in extended trading.
The world's richest person, Musk, owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and just under half of SpaceX, and analysts have said a merger would give him control of the combined entity.
The talks started in recent weeks and could result in SpaceX acquiring Tesla, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters, who declined to be named because they were not authorized to talk to the media.
Tesla has been working with an investment bank to advise on the discussions, the person said.
SpaceX's revenue climbed 161% to $14.58 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30 from a year earlier.
AI revenue surged by almost 10 times to $7.56 billion, mostly from renting out data-center capacity to developers such as Anthropic, Alphabet's Google and Reflection AI rather than from its own models.
The third quarter offered the clearest evidence yet that SpaceX’s heavy investment in AI is translating into revenue, even as spending on compute infrastructure remains enormous - capital expenses nearly tripled to $19.6 billion.
The shift is reshaping a company whose financial engine has long been its Starlink internet services business and whose longer-term ambitions still hinge on getting Starship rockets into regular service. For now, though, its main business looks closer to a cloud provider's than an AI lab's.
SpaceX's chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said the company expects $35 billion to $40 billion in capital expenditure in the fourth quarter.
"SpaceX delivered the quarter the bulls wanted, at least on the top line," said Will Rhind, CEO of asset manager GraniteShares. "The story now is all about AI. The compute contracts signed earlier this year are turning into revenue faster than a lot of people thought."
The company's AI business spans Grok, social media platform X and a fast-growing data-center operation. The business also turned a profit in the third quarter, compared with a year-ago loss.
SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion versus a net loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier and analysts' expectation for a profit of $1.57 billion. On a per-share, adjusted basis, it earned 45 cents according to IBES calculations, outstripping a 13-cent average estimate.
The satellite-internet unit has continued to expand its subscriber base, aided by additional satellite launches and a growing range of consumer, enterprise, aviation, maritime and government services.
Starlink reached 13.6 million subscribers in the third quarter, above the 12.19 million analysts expected, but growth is coming at a price: Average monthly revenue per subscriber has fallen from $99 in 2023 to $69 in the third quarter as it expands abroad with cheaper plans.
The company has said geographic expansion beyond the wealthiest countries could push average revenue per user lower over time.
Starship, SpaceX's next-generation reusable rocket system, has yet to enter commercial service. It is expected to enable deployment of higher-bandwidth Starlink satellites and orbital AI-computing infrastructure. The company's ability to turn Starship into a reliably reusable vehicle is central to its longer-term strategy.
The space segment includes commercial launches, government missions, and Starship development and remains a significant source of costs and uncertainty.

Elon Musk said that a merger between SpaceX and Tesla would be a “good idea”, adding that special committees had been formed to discuss the possibility. If the deal goes through, the combined company could be worth around $3.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
Shares of the space and technology company rose 8% in extended trading following the news. Tesla shares also gained 2% after trading slightly lower for several weeks.
Musk says SpaceX-Tesla merger is ‘good idea’
Speculation about SpaceX acquiring Tesla has grown in recent weeks. Last week, Barclays suggested that an announcement could come before Tesla's annual meeting in December.
Musk confirmed the discussions publicly for the first time, telling investors during a conference call, “I think it would be a good idea, but it's really up to the special committees of both companies…Because I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions of the special committees,”.

Why Musk would merge SpaceX and Tesla
Tesla, which makes electric vehicles, and SpaceX, which develops rockets and space technology, were once viewed as separate businesses. However, their operations increasingly overlap as Musk expands into artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing, satellite communications and computing infrastructure.
Bringing the companies together would create a single business spanning AI, energy, robotics, communications and transportation, both on Earth and beyond. The move would align their operations with Musk's long-term vision for an integrated technology and manufacturing empire.
A merger could also make it easier to take decisions. Many of Musk's projects involve multiple companies and require approval from separate boards and shareholders. Combining the businesses could give management greater flexibility to direct funding, engineering expertise and infrastructure towards projects it considers the most promising.
Musk has long argued that he needs greater control over Tesla to advance its AI and robotics plans. He owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and has voting control at SpaceX. A merger could bring his influence over the two companies under one structure.

Geopolitical concerns and regulatory scrutiny could pose major obstacles to the deal.

Shareholder approval and corporate governance would also present challenges. Investors would need convincing that bringing the two businesses together would create more value than allowing them to operate independently. Questions over conflicts of interest, voting rights and how capital would be allocated are also likely to arise.

SpaceX reported its first profit as a public company Tuesday, recording $4.4 billion in net income as well as large third-quarter revenue gains, reflecting a trifecta of growth in its launch, communications and artificial intelligence businesses.
Founder Elon Musk also disclosed that the company and electric automaker Tesla have formed special committees to explore a potential merger, which would rank as the largest of all time.
“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies,” Musk, the chief executive of both companies, said on SpaceX’s earnings webcast. “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”
After years of delays, Elon Musk demonstrated the new Tesla Roadster in Texas on Thursday. Production won’t actually begin until 2028.
Musk said he isn’t participating in the committee discussions because he is a conflicted party, and that the committees have yet to agree on terms. There has been widespread speculation on Wall Street of such a move.
The news sent SpaceX shares up $1.71, or nearly 8%, to $159.50 in after-hours trading. Tesla climbed 1.2%.
The disclosure came after a stellar earnings announcement by the Texas rocket, internet and artificial intelligence company that easily beat analysts’ net-income estimates of $1.88 billion for the company’s third quarter that ended Sept. 30. It was a swing from a $1.1-billion net loss a year earlier.
Revenue totaled $14.6 billion, nearly double the $7.8 billion second quarter figure. Capital expenditures hit $19.59 billion, mainly for AI computing, in which SpaceX is competing with OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI leaders.
“Our business is experiencing extremely strong momentum across all three segments,” President Gywnne Shotwell said in an investors presentation that was livestreamed on X and featured a video highlighting the most recent flight of its massive Starship rocket Sept. 28.
The big revenue earner for the company was its AI division, which the company has renamed as its “Super Intelligence” business, in line with President Trump’s decision in September to rebrand the entire industry.
The division recorded operating income of $431 million for the quarter on revenue of $7.56 billion, reversing a $1.26-billion loss in the second quarter on $2.56 billion in revenue.
The connectivity segment — which includes its lucrative Starlink satellite internet service — reported an operating profit of $2.37 billion on revenue of $5.25 billion, with both figures topping second-quarter results.
The business was driven by expansion of its Starlink service, which added 1.6 million subscribers worldwide, excluding enterprise contracts. Shotwell said it is now available in 174 markets with nearly 14 million customers.
The company also is making a play to become a major mobile communications provider, buying up spectrum from other companies. Shotwell said SpaceX has 22 million mobile users worldwide, up 37% from the second quarter.
The space business featured 35 launches in the quarter, including 21 that sent more Starlink satellites into orbit, as well as others for commercial and government customers. It recorded revenue of $1.77 billion, up from $962 million in the second quarter. Losses were cut to $7 million from $542 million in the second quarter.
Musk has said SpaceX’s future success hinges on its Starship rocket, slated to carry astronauts to the moon and launch hundreds of thousands of communications satellites and orbiting data centers to power its AI ambitions.
The September test flight, its 14th from its south Texas launch site, sent the rocket into orbit for the first time but was cut short due to safety concerns.
Musk spent much of his time during the earnings call touting the Starship program, noting that despite the flight being aborted, the massive rocket was able to deploy Starlink satellites with the equivalent data capacity of 10 launches of its smaller Falcon 9 fleet.
On Starship’s next flight, he said, the plan is to capture both the rocket’s first and second stages on the launch pad, a key goal to making Starship fully reusable.
“This is a massive technology milestone,” Musk said. “The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle.”
He also predicted that by the end of next year, the company will be able to launch the rocket weekly or twice a week. Starship is key for developing the company’s AI business and SpaceX is currently building out capacity on land.
SpaceX reported having 1.7 gigawatts of computer capacity at the end of the quarter and is adding more at giant centers in Memphis, Tenn., and Mississippi. The goal is to add at least 13 more gigawatts by the end of next year, Musk said.
The centers power the company’s lucrative cloud computing services and AI business, including its newly launched Grok Bot AI agent, which Musk said was quickly gaining customers.
The earnings report — only the second since the company went public in June — came after a string of news surrounding Musk and SpaceX.
On Sunday, he posted on X that he would give a share of SpaceX to every child in the country, though he didn’t provide details. The offer was an apparent response to an announcement Sunday by Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, that it would put 5% of its shares into a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund.
Last week, the Ukranian government blamed temporary speed restrictions imposed on the country’s military grade Starlink communications network for slowing its drones network. Musk said the company had nothing to do with that. There have been reports that the U.S. government may have been behind the move.
Founded in 2002 in El Segundo, SpaceX moved its headquarters from Hawthorne to Texas in 2024. However, it retains large operations in the South Bay city and blasts off regularly from Vandenberg Space Force Base in Santa Barbara County.
Shares of the company have rebounded after a sharp drop during the summer after its June 12 IPO initial public offering of stock, which offered shares at $135. The stock closed up 19% on the first day of trading but reached a low of $104.83 in July.
In its first quarterly earnings release since its $86-billion IPO, SpaceX in August reported that it grew its revenue and sharply cut its losses while beating Wall Street estimates.
