In the first official confirmation that the companies were formally talking, Musk said special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to study the idea at the request of shareholders.
Oct 20 : Elon Musk said on Tuesday that a merger of his two companies SpaceX and Tesla would be "a good idea" and that they had formed special committees to discuss a union, sending shares of the space and technology company up 8 per cent in extended trading.
The company earlier posted its first profit as a public company and Musk said he expected annual recurring revenue of between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027, as demand for its data-center space surges thanks to the AI boom.
Musk has in the past tantalized shareholders with the idea of combining SpaceX and Tesla, citing growing overlap between them. Speculation about the space company buying the EV maker has gained traction recently, with Barclays suggesting last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla's annual meeting in December.
"I think it would be a good idea, but it's really up to the special committees of both companies," Musk said in the first official confirmation that the companies were formally talking. "Because I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions of the special committees," which comprised independent directors, he told investors on a conference call.
The companies had formed the special committees at the request of shareholders, who ultimately would need to approve a deal, he added.
"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity," he said.
Terafab, the chip manufacturing joint venture between the two companies, should produce its first test chip around May or June of next year and aims to reach volume production by the third quarter of 2028, Musk said on the call.
Musk added that it would be premature to assume a SpaceX-Tesla merger would happen, noting that the special committees had not agreed on transaction terms and may never do so. Tesla shares rose 1.8 per cent in extended trading.
The world's richest person, Musk owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and just under half of SpaceX, and analysts have said a merger would give him control of the combined entity.
The talks started in recent weeks and could result in SpaceX acquiring Tesla, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters, who declined to be named because they were not authorized to talk to media. Tesla has been working with an investment bank to advise on the discussions, the person said.
AI REVENUE DRIVES SPACEX TRANSFORMATION
SpaceX's revenue climbed 161 per cent to $14.58 billion for the three months ended September 30 from a year earlier. AI revenue surged by almost 10 times to $7.56 billion, mostly from renting out data-center capacity to developers such as Anthropic, Alphabet's Google and Reflection AI rather than from its own models.
The third quarter offered the clearest evidence yet that SpaceX’s heavy investment in AI is translating into revenue, even as spending on compute infrastructure remains enormous — capital expenses nearly tripled to $19.6 billion.
The shift is reshaping a company whose financial engine has long been its Starlink internet services business and whose longer-term ambitions still hinge on getting Starship rockets into regular service. For now, though, its main business looks closer to a cloud provider's than an AI lab's.
SpaceX's chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said the company expects $35 billion to $40 billion in capital expenditure in the fourth quarter.
"SpaceX delivered the quarter the bulls wanted, at least on the top line," said Will Rhind, CEO of asset manager GraniteShares. "The story now is all about AI. The compute contracts signed earlier this year are turning into revenue faster than a lot of people thought."
The company's AI business spans Grok, social media platform X and a fast-growing data-center operation. The business also turned a profit in the third quarter, compared with a year-ago loss.
SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion versus a net loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier and analysts' expectation for a profit of $1.57 billion. On a per-share, adjusted basis, it earned 45 cents according to IBES calculations, outstripping a 13-cent average estimate.
STARLINK SUBSCRIBERS TOP FORECASTS
The satellite-internet unit has continued to expand its subscriber base, aided by additional satellite launches and a growing range of consumer, enterprise, aviation, maritime and government services.
Starlink reached 13.6 million subscribers in the third quarter, above the 12.19 million analysts expected, but growth is coming at a price: average monthly revenue per subscriber has fallen from $99 in 2023 to $69 in the third quarter as it expands abroad with cheaper plans.
The company has said geographic expansion beyond the wealthiest countries could push average revenue per user lower over time.
Starship, SpaceX's next-generation reusable rocket system, has yet to enter commercial service. It is expected to enable deployment of higher-bandwidth Starlink satellites and orbital AI-computing infrastructure. The company's ability to turn Starship into a reliably reusable vehicle is central to its longer-term strategy.
The space segment includes commercial launches, government missions and Starship development and remains a significant source of costs and uncertainty.

He added that a merger would be “a good idea,” and that “there’s a lot to be gained” from the two companies cooperating on AI software development, chip design and robotics.
As a “conflicted party,” Musk said, he cannot be a part of the committee discussions. Historically, Tesla shareholders have broadly fallen in line with Musk’s wishes, however.
The comments appeared to be the most forceful Musk has made publicly. When asked about a potential deal following SpaceX’s blockbuster July IPO, Musk didn’t offer an opinion one way or another, saying “obviously… we can’t talk about combining companies and that kind of thing on an earnings call. It’s got to be done with the appropriate process.”
Tesla shares rose more than 2% Wednesday morning.
Investors were also cheering SpaceX’s better-than-expected earnings report. The rocket, satellite internet and AI company brought in net income of $4.4 billion in the most recent quarter, swinging to a profit after back-to-back quarters of losses this year.
In its second earnings report since going public, SpaceX said it brought in $14.6 billion — up 161% year-over-year, according to the company, driven by what it called its “Super Intelligence” segment and its Starlink satellite-internet business.
Wall Street analysts surveyed by FactSet had expected net income of $1.57 billion, with revenue of $12.9 billion. SpaceX reported earnings per share of 35 cents Tuesday, versus 14 cents forecast by analysts.
Ukraine questions cloud SpaceX
Moments before the earnings call Tuesday, the Wall Street Journal published a report saying that Musk “ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink” that blindsided Ukrainian officials.
Musk during the call did not address the Journal report, which cited unnamed people familiar with the matter. CNN couldn’t immediately verify the veracity of the report.
SpaceX didn’t immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment.
Ukraine accused SpaceX last week of severely hindering its defense by suddenly limiting its Starlink internet service, which uses satellites in low orbit. Ukraine has used Starlink and a related military-grade service, Starshield, to communicate quickly and to both launch and prevent drone attacks.
While Musk repeatedly suggested the White House was to blame for the disruption, the Trump administration has denied responsibility. On X, Musk emphasized that Starshield was “owned and controlled by the US government” and that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," he said. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.
SpaceX builds space rockets as well as Starlink internet satellites and provides a secured satellite network for governments, including the US, through its Starshield business.

sources.news_title: SpaceX Earnings Preview: Equity Sees $125 Billion, Credit Sees 83 Cents
sources.text:
SpaceX Earnings Preview: Equity Sees $125 Billion, Credit Sees 83 Cents
Today after the close, SpaceX (SPCX) reports its second quarter as a public company, a day ahead of Tesla and (as Deutsche Bank puts it) "surprisingly early." The first one did not go well: the stock slid despite a big revenue beat and closed down 14% the next day, wiping out some $225 billion in market value.
This time, the sellside is mostly looking past the quarter and straight at 2027. Nobody more so than Deutsche Bank's Edison Yu, who in his preview note "Compute-driven state of mind" (available to pro subs) lifts his 2027 forecasts to $125 billion in revenue and $84 billion in EBITDA, materially above consensus of $108 billion and $65 billion. The catch, which Yu flags himself, is that those numbers are "underpinned by > $200bn in capex."
And that's where the other half of the SpaceX story comes in. While equity analysts debate how high 2027 can go, the company's 6.65% notes due 2056 just slumped to a lifetime low of 83.3 cents on the dollar, down from 98.83 at issue in June, and SpaceX's five-year CDS spreads blew out to a record high earlier this month.
In other words, the stock market is pricing the upside, and the bond market is pricing the bill.
The Quarter: In Line, With "Potential Upside In Profitability"
Start with the near term. Deutsche expects an in-line print, "with potential upside in profitability." Yu models Q3 revenue of $12.6 billion (+127% YoY), a gross margin of around 59% and EBITDA of over $6.6 billion. The engine is AI, which "is benefiting from a full-quarter contribution from cloud hosting, boosting revenue by almost 3x sequentially to ~$6bn." AI solutions & infrastructure alone is expected to jump from $2.2 billion in Q2 to $6.0 billion, which means the AI segment would account for just over half of total revenue at the business formerly known as a rocket company.
Elsewhere, consumer broadband subscribers should end the quarter at 13.5 million (vs. 12.0 million in Q2), while ARPU slides another $2 to $64, giving connectivity revenue of nearly $5 billion, up 60% YoY. The Space segment, the one in the company's name, is expected to shrink 22% YoY on twelve external Falcon 9 launches. As for the cash, Yu forecasts $19 billion in capex "mainly directed at AI compute," taking capacity to 1.8GW, and leading to free cash flow burn of $14 billion, in one quarter.
Here is the full breakdown vs. consensus:
Note that Deutsche is slightly below the Street on Q3 revenue ($12.63 billion vs. $12.89 billion) and broadband subs (13.5 million vs. 14.2 million), but slightly above on EBITDA margin (52.6% vs. 51.4%). Options are pricing a move of about 7.8% in either direction, which is a bit more than half of what the stock actually did after Q2.
How High Can 2027 Go?
This is where Deutsche gets interesting. In Yu's view, "the largest swing factor in respect to forecasts will be compute deployment." Management is targeting more than 2GW exiting 4Q26, which DB thinks is "doable," and then 5-10GW exiting 2027. DB models toward the low end, at about 6GW, and lays out a line of sight into 5-7GW of power over the next couple of years: 1.9GW of Doosan turbines, 1.2GW from the Southaven plant's 41 turbines, 0.7-1.1GW from the APR acquisition, 900MW or more leased through the Stateline JV, plus the TVA grid supply and backup turbines at Colossus 1 and up to another gigawatt "from other sources." (We assume SpaceX will need all of it to keep the Nvidia chips it is borrowing to buy switched on.)
Put it together, and the bank's math says the neocloud business alone can generate $70-90 billion of revenue in 2027, "depending on timing and pricing dynamics." For context, SpaceX's entire 2025 revenue was $18.7 billion. And the result is a 2027 forecast that is now 16% above consensus on revenue and 29% above on EBITDA:
Deutsche isn't even the most aggressive on compute. Goldman's Eric Sheridan, in his own SpaceX Q3'26 preview earlier this month (also available to pro subs), forecasts SpaceX scaling to ~2.4GW of AI compute by year-end, ~7.0GW by the end of 2027 and ~10.6GW by the end of 2028:
Goldman models $85.5 billion in 2027 AI solutions & infrastructure revenue, of which $45.5 billion comes from hosting deals on just ~1GW of contracted capacity. As we noted when we dug through Goldman's neocloud rate card, most of those hosting deals are "90-day cancellable on both sides." Which is probably worth keeping in mind when somebody extrapolates them to 2029.
Speaking of extrapolating, Musk himself already raised the bar on the Q2 call:
Musk reiterates expectation of $100 billion ARR by the end of this year (10x the June ARR), and now sees SpaceX seeing $1 trillion in revenue by 2030, and "non zero chance" of getting there in 2029. Some context: the average analyst estimate (30 of 39 sellside analysts are Buy on SPCX) for 2029 revenue is $208 billion
— zerohedge (@zerohedge) August 4, 2026
Evercore's Kutgun Maral, for one, expects an annual run rate of $104 billion by year-end and 2.3GW of compute (vs. the Street's 2.2GW), and raised his target to $270. Deutsche keeps its Buy and $235 target, vs. Friday's close of $146.03.
The $200 Billion Footnote
Here is the full set of DB's estimate changes. Look at the bottom line of each block:
Deutsche raised 2027 revenue by $10 billion, and 2027 capex by $22 billion, to $207 billion, and 2028 capex by $40 billion to $230 billion. And while 2028 revenue barely moves ($200 billion vs. $198 billion), 2028 EPS actually dips, because, as Yu admits, "there is concern by investors that pricing could normalize in 2028-29." The bank now assumes $/GW pricing "declines by 25% to about $30bn in 2028." In other words, the compute gets more expensive to build exactly when it gets cheaper to rent.
Line up DB's own EBITDA against DB's own capex, and the problem becomes obvious:
Napkin math: under Deutsche's bullish model, capex exceeds EBITDA by about $47 billion this year, $124 billion in 2027 and $81 billion in 2028, or roughly $250 billion across three years. SpaceX ended Q2 with $100 billion in cash and marketable securities, and DB expects about $13.5 billion of that to have been burned in Q3 alone. Which means the 2027 gap by itself is bigger than the cash pile... and that gap has to be filled by someone.
That someone, of course, is the bond market.
Meanwhile, In Credit...
Regular readers will recall that SpaceX slammed head first into the bond market less than two weeks after its record $86 billion IPO, selling $25 billion of investment grade bonds which were, depending on who you asked, "4x oversubscribed." Bondholders have been underwater pretty much since the break, and on Monday the 6.65% notes of 2056 hit a new all-time low of 83.345:
At that price, the 30-year paper of a BBB-rated company that is supposedly about to post $84 billion in EBITDA yields roughly 8.1%, which is the kind of number one usually associates with the junk bond market (as we put it back in August, "SPCX bonds skeptical about the $1 trillion in revenue"). The 5.875% notes due 2036 tell the same story: per Trace, their spread was 193bps earlier this month, vs. 140bps when they were sold in June.
What changed? The record chip-collateralized loan. On Oct 6, the FT reported that SpaceX wants to raise another $40 billion, about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion of IG debt, in a deal led by Apollo, to pay for Nvidia chips. Add the $25 billion from June, and SpaceX will have borrowed (or tried to borrow) $65 billion since June, on top of the $38.4 billion in debt it reported as of June 30. The next day, five-year CDS jumped as much as 16.7bps to about 197.6bps, the highest since the swaps started actively trading in June (when they were around 110bps):
Of course, we covered it at the time:
Barclays' credit analysts, led by Andrew Keches, argued that an SPV structure might be good for SpaceX in the long run by reducing the amount of debt at the parent company, but warned that in the near term the coming supply could put pressure on the company's existing bonds.
Well, they were right about the near term: less than two weeks later, the bonds are 1.4 points lower than where they were on Oct 7, and DB's revised capex forecast suggests $40 billion won't be the last ask. Or as Coherence Credit's Sal Naro told Bloomberg, speaking of AI debt in general: "This is unprecedented debt supply with no real ending in sight."
None of this will surprise those who have been reading us since last October, when we first warned that AI had quietly become a debt bubble too, and that the debt would sooner or later have to compete with everyone else (including Uncle Sam) for the same duration buyers. SpaceX, which Musk said in December had been cash-flow positive for years and didn't really need anyone's money, is now one of the biggest borrowers in that line.
What To Watch Today After The Close
Deutsche's own list of "other areas of focus" is a good checklist:
- AI: neocloud pricing and new contracts, the Cursor contribution, Grok Bot adoption, and the data center capex outlook (read: any hint that 2027 capex starts with a "2").
- Launch: timing of the next few launches after Flight 14; Flight 15 looks set for mid-/late November, though DB doesn't expect a second-stage catch.
- Connectivity: after the $8 billion Grain spectrum deal, "additional color on management's next move(s) in the US (build vs. buy)," which is something the wireless carriers will be listening to closely.
- Tesla merger: DB sees the timing as "mainly a function of valuation differentials and politics (may want to avoid a potential Democrat-led administration taking over post Trump)."
To that we'd add one more: anything on financing. Specifically, whether the $40 billion Apollo deal is done, how much of it sits in an SPV, and how much more is coming. And, after today's pledge of a SpaceX share to "every kid in America," maybe also how many shares that is.
Who Blinks First?
Deutsche's long-term thesis (as well as everyone else's for that matter) is straightforward: "the endgame is to build and possess the greatest amount of compute at the lowest cost on the ground and eventually in orbit," which should eventually let SpaceX "deliver leading intelligence/inference capabilities which we think investors generally are still quite skeptical about." Yu also concedes that "the stock has increasingly traded more in line with the AI cohort as opposed to Space." Morgan Stanley's Adam Jonas, who has become the bank's resident in house SpaceX cheerleader and now covers only this company, thinks SpaceX "looks unusually cheap" on the forward (duh), recently described the skepticism even more vividly: asked who owned the stock, out of 40 clients "not a single hand went up."
So who is right: the equity analysts who see 2027 EBITDA nearly 30% above consensus, or the bondholders who are demanding 8% for 30 years? Probably both, in their own way.
The upside case is real, but every dollar of DB's 2027 EBITDA comes with roughly two and a half dollars of capex attached, and that capex will be funded by the same creditors who just marked the 2056s to 83. If today's call brings a higher capex number and no clarity on financing, we suspect the bond market will be the one setting the tone, just as it did after Q2. Then again, Musk has never been shy about telling bears that he "tried to warn them," and as of Friday's close the stock was still 8% above its $135 IPO price. The bonds, meanwhile, are almost 16% below theirs.
Much more in the full Deutsche Bank "Compute-driven state of mind" note and Goldman's "SpaceX Q3'26 preview," both available to pro subs.

sources.news_title: Tesla Sets December 3 Shareholder Meeting Amid Rumors of an Imminent SpaceX Merger
sources.text:
October was hailed as one of the most consequential months of 2026 for Tesla and Elon Musk's other companies. The carmaker has unveiled a second variant of the Roadster that can fly, roll, and land, a PR stunt seen as a warm-up for a possible SpaceX-Tesla merger. Both companies are holding their third-quarter earnings calls this week, with SpaceX on Tuesday and Tesla on Wednesday. For SpaceX, this also comes after a successful Starship launch on September 28.
Unsurprisingly, Elon Musk is looking to bank on these successes with an anticipated announcement of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Days before the third-quarter earnings call, Tesla called the annual shareholder meeting on December 3. The official agenda doesn't mention the merger, but that is still looming large and will likely be discussed during the meeting.
Officially, the shareholder meeting has three proposals on the ballot, and none is about the merger. Tesla wants its shareholders to re-elect Elon Musk, Robyn Denholm, and JB Straubel to Tesla's Board of Directors and to approve PwC as Tesla's auditor for 2026. Shareholders are also asked to vote on 2025 executive compensation, including about $158.4 billion in 2025 stock awards to Musk.
Elon Musk hasn't ruled out a merger between SpaceX and Tesla, but has said in the past that an earnings call was not the place to discuss it. This would be the role of a shareholder meeting. If we don't see the merger talks mentioned in the proxy statement, it's because Tesla can't hold a vote until it fulfills certain requirements, which include informing the shareholders about this intention.
The proxy statement does include some hints at such a move, if that was not clear enough already. For instance, the statement confirms that Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs both Tesla's compensation committee and its governance committee, is also a member of the SpaceX board since February. Another sign is even clearer to pave the way for a future merger: automatic voting.
Specifically, the meeting marks the debut of Tesla's Voluntary Retail Voting Program, which essentially locks investor votes with the board for future votes. There are two options, with one being to vote your shares with the board on everything, while the second leaves out so-called "special matters," including director elections or mergers that need shareholder approval. There's no option to auto-vote against the board.
This means that shareholders who pick "All Matters" when opting for the program will have their shares automatically counted for the board's position on a merger. This should make it easier to pass a vote and avoid an embarrassment like the one cast in November 2025. Back then, the Tesla board attempted to eliminate the supermajority voting requirements, but couldn't get enough shares to pass the bar. While the auto-vote mandate does not apply to the December 3 vote, it will count in the next shareholder meeting.
There are several indications that Tesla and SpaceX are preparing to announce a merger. Musk has been trying for a long time to tie the two companies in joint projects, and last week's Roadster PR stunt is but an example. Immediately following the event, SpaceX executives have started following Tesla social media accounts and vice versa, supposedly for more than just seeing their Halloween posts.
Analysts expect the SpaceX earnings call tonight and Tesla's tomorrow to provide a clearer picture of what a Tesla-SpaceX merger will look like. The most likely scenario is an all-stock deal, with SpaceX buying Tesla at a premium. This means that Tesla shares will convert into SpaceX stock, and the third-quarter results will effectively set the price for this conversion.

SpaceX investors, ahead of results, press Musk on Tesla merger
SpaceX shareholders want to know when the rocket maker will merge with Tesla, bringing together two of Elon Musk’s biggest companies in a union that investors have long speculated about.
“When will SpaceX merge with Tesla?” was the second-most upvoted question – drawing 26 upvotes – submitted by investors to SpaceX management ahead of its third-quarter earnings webcast on Tuesday. The same question received 128 upvotes on the Tesla investor relations site.
Barclays suggested last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla’s annual meeting, with SpaceX the likelier acquirer, though neither company nor Musk has officially committed to favoring a deal.
Lunar lander progress questioned
The top-voted question, with 38 upvotes, was on the progress of Starship’s lunar lander hardware, in a list that showed retail investors were focused on Starship while analysts and institutional shareholders pressed for detail on AI revenue and spending.
SpaceX has made progress testing Starship, but key technologies needed to turn the giant rocket into a lunar lander, including refueling it in orbit, have yet to be fully demonstrated. The company’s profitable satellite internet service, Starlink, is helping bankroll heavy spending on chips, terrestrial data centers and Grok, but losses at the AI businesses have ballooned.
While the investor questions list ahead of its second-quarter earnings in August was topped by lighthearted, meme-driven submissions, this quarter’s top questions leaned more toward corporate plans, with novelty entries mostly near the bottom.
“What share of AI revenue is now under multi-year commitments, and what gives management confidence AI can grow at or above the company’s overall rate for several years?” A prospective investor asked, earning no upvotes. SpaceX’s AI revenue comes from a handful of customers, including Alphabet’s Google and AI lab Anthropic, and the compute contracts can be terminated on about 90 days’ notice.
One institutional investor asked how much contracted Google capacity would stay available if a court halted gas turbines at the Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, Tennessee. Another asked whether Google had accepted the full capacity under its cloud agreement and whether SpaceX expected to earn the full contractual monthly rate.
An analyst’s six-part question on Starlink satellite capacity, launch priorities and capital spending drew no upvotes.
Lighter submissions were scattered through the list. One user asked whether SpaceX would land a Tesla Roadster – a sports car with rocket thrusters for short jumps in the air – on the moon, adding, “(it) would be awesome.”

Some investors believe a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla could offer structural advantages, including a way to address Tesla’s Chinese operations separately.

sources.news_title: Tesla asks shareholders to re-elect Musk, Denholm and Straubel at December annual meeting
Tesla (TSLA) proxy shows a board getting ready for a SpaceX merger
sources.text:
Tesla’s proxy for its 2026 annual meeting, filed today, confirms that one of its supposedly independent directors now sits on SpaceX’s board. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs both Tesla’s compensation committee and its governance committee, joined SpaceX’s board in February.
That’s one of several details in the filing that line up with a Tesla-SpaceX merger. There’s a three-item ballot, an auto-voting program that kicks in for the next vote, and Musk pay terms that pay out on a deal price alone.
Three items, no shareholder proposals
Tesla’s 2026 annual meeting is set for December 3 at Gigafactory Texas, for shareholders of record as of October 13.
They get three things to vote on. The first is re-electing Elon Musk, board chair Robyn Denholm and JB Straubel to three-year terms. The second is a non-binding say-on-pay vote, and the third is ratifying PwC as Tesla’s auditor, a job it has held since 2005.
That’s it. No shareholder proposals made the ballot this year. At least, not yet. Last year’s meeting featured several, including one asking the board to invest in xAI, which has since been absorbed by SpaceX.
The board also says it won’t bring back proposals to declassify itself or to drop Tesla’s supermajority voting requirements. Its 2025 attempt drew 73.6% participation but only 39.4% of outstanding shares in support, short of the bar. So the staggered board stays, and the three directors up this year would serve until 2029.
Denholm’s letter makes the pitch directly, telling shareholders that “a steady and experienced hand during this time of rapid technological change is essential to Tesla’s success.”
As chair, Denholm has long been criticized for letting Elon Musk do what he wants, unchecked by the board, but with Musk’s backing, it’s doubtful Tesla shareholders can get her out.
Musk’s 2025 pay: $158 billion on paper
The say-on-pay item asks shareholders to approve Musk’s 2025 compensation, which the proxy reports at $158,359,009,867. Against a median Tesla employee who made $62,786, that’s a CEO pay ratio of 2,522,203 to 1.
None of that was cash. The figure combines $132.3 billion for the 2025 CEO Performance Award, valued as if every milestone gets hit, and $26.1 billion for the August 2025 “interim award.” Musk forfeited the interim award in April after the Delaware Supreme Court reinstated his 2018 package.
Tesla adds its own “realized compensation” table showing Musk received $0 in 2025, for a pay ratio of “0.00:1.” Accurate for 2025. But the same proxy discloses that on June 16, 2026, Musk exercised all 303,960,630 of his 2018 options, covering the $23.34 exercise price by having Tesla withhold 17,531,857 shares. That implies a share price of about $405 and a value of roughly $116 billion at exercise.
Tesla’s income statement tells a third story. The 2025 award has generated $689 million in stock-based compensation expense so far: $162 million in 2025 and $527 million in the first half of 2026. Tesla only books expense for milestones it considers “probable,” and out of 12 operational milestones it rates exactly one as probable: 20 million cumulative vehicle deliveries.
FSD subscriptions, Optimus, robotaxis and every EBITDA target sit in the “not probable” bucket, worth $105.8 billion to $120.4 billion in unrecognized expense.
All of this comes after a year where Tesla’s net income fell 46% to $3.86 billion and revenue declined for a second straight year, to $94.8 billion.
How a merger pays Musk
As we noted when Tesla got the SEC’s OK to auto-vote retail shares, the 2025 award works differently in a change in control. The filings lay out exactly how.
Normally, each of the 12 tranches needs a market cap milestone, measured as a trailing average over six months and 30 days, plus an operational milestone. In a change in control, operational milestones drop out. Tesla’s market cap gets measured once: shares outstanding multiplied by the higher of the last closing price or the per-share value shareholders receive in the deal. Any tranche earned that way vests immediately instead of after 7.5 to 10 years.
With 3.95 billion shares outstanding, the first $2 trillion tranche works out to about $506 per share. A deal valuing Tesla at $3 trillion, or about $759 per share, would earn Musk three tranches, or 105.9 million shares, without a single robotaxi or Optimus milestone.
The April 2026 Implementation Agreement for the 2018 package follows the same logic. The 286.4 million restricted shares Musk received from the June exercise don’t vest until January 19, 2028. A change in control while he’s still CEO, or running product or operations, vests them right away.
Whether a Tesla-SpaceX combination would count as a change in control depends on how it’s structured. But both of Musk’s packages are now built to pay out fast if it does.
The auto-vote button arrives
This meeting is also the launch of Tesla’s “Voluntary Retail Voting Program.” Retail shareholders who vote through ProxyVote or Robinhood will be offered enrollment in a standing instruction for all future meetings.
There are two options. The first votes your shares with the board on everything. The second votes with the board on everything except a “Special Matter,” which Tesla defines as a contested director election or a merger, acquisition or divestiture that needs shareholder approval.
There’s no option to vote against the board. Shareholders who pick “all matters” will have their shares counted for the board’s position on a merger unless they log in and override it. Tesla’s only commitment is a reminder before that meeting.
The instructions don’t apply to the December 3 vote. They start with the next shareholder meeting, which is where a SpaceX deal would land.
Three of nine directors tied to SpaceX
Ehrenpreis isn’t the only link. Elon Musk runs SpaceX, and his brother Kimbal Musk, also a Tesla director, has served on SpaceX’s board. That’s a third of Tesla’s nine-member board.
Tesla’s board still classifies Ehrenpreis as independent. As chair of the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee, his job description includes “considering questions of possible conflicts of interest of Tesla’s directors and officers.”
Tesla is also a SpaceX shareholder now. Its $2 billion investment in xAI converted into SpaceX Class A stock after SpaceX acquired xAI Holdings in February, and the purchase closed on March 12. The SpaceX S-1 put that stake at 18,990,195 shares, under 1% of the company.
The money flows the other way too. Tesla’s proxy shows $430.1 million in 2025 revenue from xAI, mostly Megapacks, and another $143.3 million from SpaceX, mostly vehicles.
On the Q2 earnings call in July, Musk said a combination would have to “be done with the appropriate process.”
Electrek’s Take
Ehrenpreis has been on Tesla’s board since 2007. The 2018 changes came out of the Tornetta mess. And the auto-vote program is sold as a fix for low retail turnout.
Top comment by Beario
Seems to be a lot going on to ensure that this merger happens without a hitch including SpaceX stock promised to every child in America added to their Trump accounts as a gift. Its not a joke, I read that this morning that the US treasury laid out new rules for these accounts and no capital gains taxes on them. The Treasury Department is automatically enrolling up to 60 million children in the Trump Accounts program. Not sure what to make of all of these things and this new government business collaboration, but the old saying is beware of Greeks bearing gifts.
Put them side by side, though, and it reads like a checklist for a merger vote. Musk’s pay packages pay out quickly on a deal price. The director in charge of reviewing conflicts sits on the other company’s board. The board that would negotiate the deal is locked in through 2029. And retail shareholders are being offered a button that turns them into standing votes for the board, merger included, unless they pick the carve-out.
The problem is who’s on the other side of the table. Musk owns about 20% of Tesla and controls roughly 85% of SpaceX’s voting power. Whatever exchange ratio the two boards land on, he benefits from both ends of it. That’s exactly when Tesla shareholders need the most independent board possible. Instead, the board is getting closer to SpaceX, not further away.
Musk is right that this needs “the appropriate process,” but of course, he doesn’t really mean it. He has engineered Tesla’s board and shareholder base for years to answer to one person: him.

The results will test whether Starlink's steady growth and Tesla's car profits can fund the AI spending powering the merger debate.
"In terms of metrics, it would have to be Starlink revenue growth more than launch counts and improvement in auto margins for Tesla," said Shawn Campbell, an adviser at Camelthorn Investments who owns shares in both companies, describing investors' focus for results.
Barclays suggested last week a deal could be announced before Tesla's annual meeting, with SpaceX the likelier acquirer, though neither company nor Musk has officially committed to favoring a deal.
Tesla on Monday said its annual meeting would be held on December 3.
In an all-stock deal, Barclays estimates Musk would hold about 37% of the equity and 56% of the votes.
"A SpaceX acquisition of Tesla would be cleaner as it would make it easier to deal with the China business as an asset that is dealt with separately," Campbell said.
Tesla gave the speculation a showpiece on Thursday, unveiling a new Roadster sports car, slated for production in 2028, that can jump and turn over mid-air using rocket technology at a SpaceX test site in Texas.
"Musk is blending the future of mobility together by integrating auto and rocket technology; at the very least it's a subtle plant in investors' minds making an engineering efficiency argument for a merger," said Bill Birmingham, head of research at REX Financial.
He said the timing, ahead of Tesla's annual shareholders meeting, was no coincidence.
SpaceX absorbed Musk's xAI in February, months before its June IPO, and spending by Tesla and SpaceX now points to the same place: AI.
The businesses still differ, with SpaceX earning from launches, Starlink and AI compute, and Tesla from cars and energy storage.
SpaceX reports on Tuesday and Tesla on Wednesday after markets close.
SPACEX: AI SPENDING IN FOCUS
SpaceX reports only its second results as a public company, with investors watching whether its surging AI spending is turning into revenue.
The company is expected to report third-quarter revenue of about $12.74 billion and earnings of 14 cents a share, just four months after going public, according to data compiled by LSEG.
That compares with second-quarter revenue of $7.8 billion, a net loss of $541 million, and AI capital spending of $15.8 billion.
Evercore ISI expects SpaceX to exit 2026 at an annualized revenue run-rate of about $104 billion, driven by the AI segment doing "most of the heavy lifting," and estimates capital spending reaching about $151 billion in 2027.
Connectivity revenue, which includes Starlink, rose 66% to $4.3 billion in the second quarter.
SpaceX also agreed on October 8 to buy 800 MHz spectrum from Grain Management for about $8 billion, a deal that needs Federal Communications Commission approval and underpins its Starlink Mobile push.
Shares closed at $146.03 on Friday, above the $135 IPO price but well below their post-debut peak.
TESLA: ROBOTAXIS AND LONG-TERM BETS
Tesla is on track to grow deliveries this year for the first time since 2023, but investors are more focused on profits and its robotaxi bets.
Analysts expect Tesla to report adjusted earnings of roughly 43 cents a share on revenue of about $27.88 billion, compared with 50 cents a year earlier.
Second-quarter profit fell well short of estimates, with negative free cash flow of $1.1 billion — slipping into the red for the first time in over two years.
Still, Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter, beating analysts' estimates.
Tesla has said capital spending will exceed $25 billion this year, and its shares are down about 17% in 2026 as analysts expect the company to post negative free cash flow of $4.92 billion for the third quarter.
Still, Wall Street has largely focused on robotaxis and the Optimus humanoid robot to assess the company's growth, citing them as high-margin product lines that could overshadow its traditional car sales business eventually.
While Tesla's robotaxi business and fleet are small compared to Waymo, the company expects to roll out its self-driving taxis widely in the coming years.
Its valuation has largely hinged on such long-term ambitions instead of the car business, which contributes the lion's share of the company's revenue.

Elon Musk’s floated merger of SpaceX and Tesla would do more than unite rockets and electric cars. It would fold two of the world’s largest corporate Bitcoin stashes onto a single balance sheet.
Speaking on SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call Tuesday, Musk said the boards of both companies had formed special committees of independent directors to weigh a tie-up, cautioning that treating a deal as “a certainty” would be “overstating it.”

SpaceX’s third-quarter 2026 results, reported after the bell on October 20, mark the moment the company stopped being a rocket-and-satellite business with an AI side project and became an AI compute and software company that also happens to own the world’s dominant launch system and satellite broadband network. Revenue surged 161% year-over-year to $14.58 billion, comfortably ahead of the roughly $12.7 billion consensus estimate, with the newly branded Super Intelligence (SI) segment generating $7.56 billion of it, up a staggering 830% from a year earlier and, for the first time, more than half of total revenue.
Now trading under the ticker SPCX after its 2026 IPO, the company reported revenue of $14.58 billion, beating projections by roughly $1.7 billion. Adjusted EBITDA hit $8.81 billion against a consensus of about $6.6 billion, up 306% year-over-year, and the company swung to a GAAP net income of $4.4 billion from a $1.05 billion loss in the prior-year quarter, its first solidly profitable quarter since listing. Adjusted EPS of about $0.35 more than doubled Street expectations of $0.13–0.16.
The SI segment’s $6.7 billion in incremental revenue was boosted by three sources: the activation of major new cloud services agreements, the acquisition of coding platform Cursor (which closed mid-quarter and contributed $608 million), and accelerating adoption of the Grok model family, including the newly launched Grok Bot agentic system. Crucially, SI witnessed a dramatic turnaround after posting a $1.26 billion operating loss as recently as Q2; the segment turned operationally profitable at $431 million, even while absorbing $1.2 billion in Cursor-related stock compensation, and delivered $4.95 billion in adjusted EBITDA.
CFO Bret Johnsen offered a striking metric on the earnings call: at current pricing, new compute deployments are paying back in under a year, with compute pricing tracking “slightly above the high end” of 30–50 per watt. Nameplate capacity reached 1.7 GW at quarter-end, up from 0.6 GW a year ago, as construction continued on the COLOSSUS II facility.
Starlink still made strong contributions
Starlink, long SpaceX’s profit anchor, remains healthy. Connectivity revenue rose 69% year-over-year to $5.25 billion, with segment operating income up 99% to $2.37 billion. Consumer subscribers climbed to 13.6 million, up 89% from a year earlier, while ARPU ticked up 5% sequentially to $69. Starlink is now installed on more than 3,800 aircraft, and enterprise/government revenue jumped 91%.
The Space segment contributed $1.77 billion, up 6% year-over-year, highlighted by Starship Flight 14, the first revenue-generating Starship mission, which deployed 26 V3 Starlink satellites with roughly 10 times the downlink capacity of a Falcon 9 launch. SpaceX also announced Starbase, Louisiana, a next-generation spaceport targeting its first launch in 2029.
Meanwhile, it was not all uhuru; the quarter’s Capex totalled $19.6 billion, $16.4 billion of it in SI, and nine-month capital spending of $48 billion dwarfs operating cash flow of $13.1 billion. The $8.8 billion adjusted EBITDA figure also sits well above $2.8 billion in GAAP operating income, a gap worth monitoring. Still, roughly $90 billion in cash and marketable securities provides a formidable buffer.
SpaceX and Tesla merger talks
Musk confirmed on the call that both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees, composed of independent directors, formed at shareholder request, to explore a merger. Because Musk is a conflicted party in both companies, he cannot participate in the discussions. He was characteristically calibrated: “I don’t think we should necessarily assume a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty. And I think that would be overstating it. Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes.”
The strategic logic, as Ark Invest frames it, is a combined entity generating $3.8 trillion in sales by 2031, with Tesla’s robotaxi cash flows funding SpaceX’s orbital data centres and SpaceX’s compute serving as the planning layer for Optimus deployments. But governance hurdles are real: any deal would require approval from over 50% of all Tesla shares voting yes.
Musk’s guidance will fuel the debate. He projected annual recurring revenue of $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027, numbers that annualise to $55 billion-plus in 2026 but imply a growth trajectory no public company has ever sustained.
The SpaceX Q3 earnings call revealed a genuinely historic quarter. The SI segment’s 830% growth validates the SpaceXAI restructuring; the first profit validates the operating model; the merger committees validate months of speculation. The risk, capital intensity, customer concentration in AI compute, and governance complexity of merging two Musk-controlled companies remain substantial. But after Q3, the burden of proof has shifted decisively to the sceptics.

sources.news_title: Why Elon Musk Wants Tesla and SpaceX Under One Roof: Chips, AI and Orbital Data Centres - Hello Entrepreneurs
sources.text:
Elon Musk isn’t just trying to shove electric cars and rockets under one company for fun. His real goal? He wants to glue together the technologies he thinks are going to drive Tesla and SpaceX forward—stuff like artificial intelligence, cutting-edge chips, robotics, satellites, and serious data centers.
Here’s what’s happening right now: both Tesla and SpaceX set up special independent committees to see if merging makes any sense. Musk, being the boss of both, had to step back because, well, that’s a clear conflict of interest. He’s said himself that the committees haven’t agreed on anything yet, and there’s no guarantee this merger will actually happen.
At first, people thought of Tesla and SpaceX as totally separate. Tesla builds electric cars, batteries, and robots; SpaceX fires rockets and manages satellites. But lately, the two have started to look more alike. They’re both pouring money into AI, designing custom semiconductors, and building big computing infrastructure.
Musk believes there’s a lot to gain by pulling these efforts together: smarter AI, better chip design, a shared robotics platform, and a vast “Starmind” network of data centers orbiting in space. That list explains why the merger talk has gotten serious. Tesla needs horsepower for self-driving cars, robots, and AI. SpaceX needs it for satellite systems, launches, Starlink connectivity, and the wild idea of putting data centers in orbit. One company could line those priorities up better than two chasing the same tech in parallel.
The most obvious connection so far is Terafab, a chip plant under construction in Grimes County, Texas. Both companies are working on it together. The chips will power Tesla’s Optimus robots and future autonomous taxis, and also feed high-powered satellites and planned space-based data centers for SpaceX. If Musk controls chip design and production, he cuts out outside suppliers—crucial when advanced chips are at the heart of AI. Plus, it gives both companies a joint base for the critical tech they’ll both use.
What does each side get out of this? Tesla gets access to SpaceX’s rockets, satellite network, and cloud-ambitions-in-orbit. That could help Tesla’s push on self-driving tech, robots, and its AI backbone. SpaceX taps into Tesla’s battery tech, factories, and robotics expertise. Together, the whole company could cover everything from cars and robots to rockets, satellites, and telecommunications. Musk has even hinted that fusing Tesla’s robotics with SpaceX’s AI and satellite reach might eventually make better vehicles. But right now, these ideas are just that—no official roadmap, no new products announced.
Still, control is a big factor. Musk owns nearly 20% of Tesla, and he’s got voting control at SpaceX. Analysts see the merger as a way to consolidate even more power in his hands, especially given his obsession with steering Tesla’s AI and robotics agenda himself. Since he’s in charge of both, the independent committees are running the show instead.
There are huge hurdles, though. Musk himself says nothing’s set in stone. Beyond that, Tesla is a public company and SpaceX is private. Any merger faces tough questions around valuation, getting shareholders on board, sorting out governance, and satisfying regulators. And investors will want to know if Musk becomes even more powerful—plus, whether smaller shareholders get a fair shake.
Commercial risks are in the mix too. Tesla is up against tough competition in electric vehicles, and SpaceX’s move into orbital AI infrastructure and data centers is expensive and largely unproven. Smashing the two together combines those risks, instead of letting investors pick and choose.
If this ever happens, you’d end up with one of the world’s weirdest and most ambitious tech companies—cars, energy storage, robots, rockets, satellites, telecoms, and AI all in one place. That’s the kind of empire Musk clearly wants.
But honestly, the real question is whether there’s enough upside in chips, AI, and orbital computing to justify merging two giants with totally different businesses, investors, and risks. Right now, it’s just an idea being examined, and not even Musk is claiming it’s a done deal.

Musk made the announcement during SpaceX’s third quarter earnings call when an investor asked him directly about a possible combination. He said each company had set up a special committee to look at the idea, and he called a merger “a good idea.”
A special committee is a small group of board members brought in when a company’s leader has a personal stake on both sides of a deal. Musk runs both Tesla and SpaceX, so if he negotiated the terms himself, he would essentially be making a deal with himself. That is why these committees are made up only of independent directors, meaning board members with no financial conflict in the outcome.
“These special committees consist of independent directors, and because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” Musk said. He described the process as “an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation,” comparing it to the highly choreographed style of Japanese theater.
Musk also tried to cool expectations. “Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said. He added that the committees were formed at the request of shareholders, and that on Tesla’s side a deal would need support from a majority of all outstanding shares, which he called “quite a high hurdle.” In plain terms, it is not enough for most of the people who show up to vote to say yes. More than half of every Tesla share in existence has to back it.
The money involved is staggering. At Tuesday’s closing prices, SpaceX was worth about $2 trillion and Tesla close to $1.5 trillion. Combined, that would be the largest corporate merger ever recorded. Shares of both companies jumped in after hours trading following the news.
A Tesla SpaceX merger would put Tesla’s electric cars, batteries and humanoid robots under the same roof as SpaceX’s rockets, its Starlink satellite internet service and its artificial intelligence business. Tesla supplies batteries and manufacturing technology for some SpaceX projects, and the companies are jointly building Terafab, a facility designed to make AI chips.
SpaceX only became a publicly traded company in June, when it went public on the Nasdaq in a record $75 billion initial public offering, the first time everyday investors could buy its stock. That number has not been set, and no deal terms have been agreed to.
Tesla shareholders have been here before. In 2016, Tesla bought SolarCity, a solar company Musk was also heavily invested in, through a similar special committee process, and shareholders fought that deal in court for years. Tesla investors are also already tied up in legal disputes over the company’s investment in xAI.
Wall Street is largely betting it happens anyway. Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, put the odds of a merger within two years at 95 percent. A combined entity would represent one of the largest corporate mergers in history.
Stock Market Response
SpaceX shares rose 8% in after-hours trading following Musk’s comments.
Tesla shares rose 2% after a recent dip, reflecting investor interest in Musk’s strategic direction.
Background: Why the Idea Exists
Musk has increasingly integrated his companies under shared goals.
Before going public, SpaceX acquired xAI and X (formerly Twitter), both of which Musk owned.
Earlier this year, Tesla and SpaceX jointly launched Terafab — a project focused on manufacturing computer chips.
This collaboration signals a growing alignment in their work on artificial intelligence, software, and chip development.
Why a Merger Might Make Sense
Musk argued that combining Tesla and SpaceX could enhance efficiency in AI and chip development.
Both companies are advancing in areas like robotics and AI infrastructure.
SpaceX has outperformed Tesla in market valuation since its public debut.
Shareholder Approval Required
Any merger would require approval from at least 50% of Tesla’s shareholders.
Musk described this as a "quite high hurdle to achieve."
Historically, Tesla shareholders have supported Musk’s initiatives — including a $1 trillion compensation package approved last year.
Limitations and Open Questions
There is no official plan or timeline for the merger.
Shareholders may be hesitant due to the complexity and scale of such a deal.
Musk is not a member of either special committee, maintaining a formal separation between his roles.
While the idea is under review, it remains speculative and not binding.

sources.news_title: Tesla and SpaceX are exploring a merger, and Musk says it’s about superintelligence
sources.text:
Elon Musk’s Tesla Roadster, with the “Starman” mannequin in a SpaceX spacesuit at the wheel, after SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy demo launch in February 2018 (file photo). Image: SpaceX / Wikimedia Commons, CC0 1.0 (public domain), cropped
Tesla and SpaceX have each set up special board committees to explore merging the two companies, Elon Musk said on SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings webcast on Tuesday, and he made the case for a deal in terms of building superintelligence.
Musk, who runs both companies, said the committees are made up of independent directors and have not agreed any terms. He called a combination “a good idea”, but said it was far from certain and would need the backing of Tesla’s shareholders. Neither company had filed a statement about the committees with the US Securities and Exchange Commission by Tuesday evening.
“An odd kabuki dance”
Musk said he is not on either committee and is not part of the talks. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” he said. “So it’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation.”
The question was already on investors’ minds. “When will SpaceX merge with Tesla?” was among the questions shareholders submitted on SpaceX’s Q&A platform ahead of the call. In January, before SpaceX bought Elon Musk’s AI lab xAI instead, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX had weighed a merger with Tesla as an alternative.
Making the case for a deal, Musk put AI first:
I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity. And there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the TeraFab, obviously robotics, mass to orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity.
Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, on SpaceX’s Q3 2026 earnings webcast
A high bar at Tesla
Musk was careful not to oversell it. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this,” he said. “And particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50 percent vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that’s quite a high hurdle to try to achieve.”
That means a deal would need more than half of every Tesla share, including those held by investors who never vote, not just a majority of the votes cast. Any terms would come from the two committees first and then go to shareholders. Tesla reports its own third-quarter results after the US market closes on Wednesday, October 21.
Two companies already sharing AI
The deal Musk described would put most of his AI bets under one roof. SpaceX’s AI unit, now called Super Intelligence and home to Grok and the coding company Cursor, took in $7.56 billion in the third quarter, more than Starlink, according to the results SpaceX filed earlier on Tuesday. Tesla’s own AI work centres on its Optimus humanoid robots, Full Self-Driving and robotaxis.
The two companies are already tangled together. Tesla invested $2 billion in xAI, a stake that became SpaceX shares when the two merged, and SpaceX’s AI unit spent about $430 million on Tesla Megapack batteries last year, CNBC reported. Musk said on the call that SpaceX aims to reach volume production of AI chips, developed with Tesla and Intel, at its planned Terafab factory in Texas in the third quarter of 2028. Teslas now carry SpaceXAI’s Grok Bot, and the two firms are jointly building Digital Optimus, a computer-use AI that Musk says can play games by watching the screen. Tesla is also building hundreds of Optimus robots a week.
Why it matters
A merger would join the company behind Grok and Cursor with the one building Optimus robots and robotaxis, giving Musk one balance sheet for chips, data centres and AI he says is heading for superintelligence. It is still only an idea in committee, and the vote it needs at Tesla is a hard one to win.

Table of Contents
American billionaire Elon Musk said SpaceX and Tesla Inc. have each set up special committees of independent directors to study a merger of the two companies, a combination that would bring together businesses worth about $3.5 trillion and rank as the largest corporate deal on record.
Musk, who runs both companies, disclosed the talks on Tuesday during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings webcast. He said he favors a deal but has been kept out of the discussions because he controls both sides.
"Because I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions," Musk said. "I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies."
The committees have not agreed on terms, and Musk cautioned investors against treating a deal as settled. "Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty," he said. "I think that would be overstating it."
SpaceX has a stock market value of about $2 trillion, and Tesla is worth close to $1.5 trillion. SpaceX shares rose 4.6% in after-hours trading following the results, while Tesla gained 1.2%.
What a deal would combine
A merger would put Tesla's electric car, battery and humanoid robot businesses under the same roof as SpaceX's rockets, its Starlink satellite internet service and its artificial intelligence operations. "There's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software," Musk said. Both companies are spending heavily on AI, from data centers to self-driving cars.
The two companies already do business with each other. SpaceX has bought more than $100 million worth of Tesla Cybertrucks, and Musk's AI company xAI, which SpaceX absorbed in February, is a large buyer of Tesla's utility-scale batteries. SpaceX considered a combination with Tesla early this year before deciding to merge with xAI instead, in a deal that valued SpaceX at $1 trillion and xAI at $250 billion.
Any merger would need the backing of Tesla's shareholders. Musk said the deal would require the approval of a majority of all Tesla shares outstanding, rather than a majority of the votes cast, which he described as a high bar. Tesla holds its annual meeting on Dec. 3.
Analysts at Barclays told clients earlier this month that a deal could be announced before that meeting. Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, put the odds of a merger within two years at 95%.
SpaceX swings to a profit
Musk spoke as SpaceX reported its first quarterly operating profit since its record initial public offering in June. Revenue jumped 161% from a year earlier to $14.6 billion in the three months to September, beating analysts' estimates of about $12.9 billion. Operating income came to $2.79 billion, compared with an operating loss of $143 million in the second quarter.
The company's AI business, which rents computing power to customers including Anthropic, Google and X, generated $7.56 billion in revenue, almost triple the previous quarter and well ahead of Starlink. Revenue from the connectivity unit, which is mostly Starlink, rose 69% to $5.25 billion. The rocket launch business grew 6% to $1.77 billion. SpaceX spent $19.6 billion on equipment and other capital projects in the quarter.
Tesla reports its own third-quarter results on Wednesday.
Musk's stakes
Musk is the largest shareholder in both companies. He held 48.4% of SpaceX as of June 30, including shares that vest only if the company hits performance targets, and he controls more than 82% of its voting power. He is also Tesla's biggest investor. The two holdings make up most of a fortune that has made him the world's richest person.
How the two stakes would be blended in a merger, and how much of the combined company Musk would control, would depend on the exchange ratio the committees agree on. Musk has said in the past that he wants enough voting power at Tesla to keep control over the company's AI and robotics work.

sources.news_title: Tesla & SpaceX Earnings Preview: Two Reports, One Merger Question — What Are Options Pricing?

Elon Musk’s Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX (SPCX) report earnings on consecutive evenings this week, but growing merger speculation introduces an unusual wildcard for options traders.
SpaceX reports Tuesday, October 20, followed by Tesla on Wednesday. Recent Barclays commentary has fueled speculation about a potential all-stock merger, although neither company has announced a deal.
The timing creates a unique two-stage volatility event, where SpaceX’s results could influence Tesla’s trading ahead of its own report.
With options pricing roughly 6–8% moves in both stocks, can earnings and merger speculation produce reactions large enough to overcome elevated option premiums?
We examine what the options market is pricing, how SpotGamma’s dealer positioning and volatility signals compare, and which defined-risk strategies may offer attractive opportunities.
1. What the Options Market Is Pricing
Both companies enter earnings with substantial event risk embedded in their options.
SpaceX’s options are pricing a move of approximately 8.0%, compared with roughly 5.5% for Tesla. The latter of which has decreased since last week.
These are substantial expectations, although neither would be unprecedented.
SpaceX declined approximately 13.6% following its previous earnings report, while Tesla suffered a 14.5% drop after its July results.
Historically, Tesla has demonstrated considerable earnings volatility. Over its last eight quarterly reports, its median absolute reaction was approximately 4.5%, compared with an average closer to 7.8%, reflecting occasional outsized moves.
The takeaway: Both names are pricing significant volatility, but the distribution of potential outcomes remains highly sensitive to unexpected guidance and merger-related headlines.
Importantly, the straddle-implied range extends through Friday expiration and includes ordinary trading movement beyond the earnings announcements themselves.
2. What Wall Street Expects
While the merger rumors may dominate headlines, both companies face meaningful fundamental tests.
SpaceX: Can AI Growth Justify the Spending?
SpaceX enters its second earnings announcement since its June IPO with investors focused on the expansion of Starlink and its increasingly ambitious AI infrastructure business.
Last quarter, the company reported approximately $7.8 billion in revenue but spent $18.4 billion on capital expenditures, including $15.8 billion on AI computing infrastructure.
Investors will be closely watching Starlink subscriber growth, AI monetization, cash burn and updated capital expenditure guidance.
Tesla: Margins Versus the Autonomous Future
Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles during the quarter, exceeding expectations, while deploying 13.7 GWh of energy storage products.
However, deliveries alone are unlikely to determine the stock’s reaction.
Automotive margins, free cash flow, and progress toward commercializing Robotaxi and Optimus remain central to Tesla’s valuation.
With annual capital spending expected to exceed $25 billion, investors are increasingly focused on how Tesla intends to finance its longer-term growth initiatives.
3. What Skew, Compass, and Dealer Gamma Reveal
Options positioning reveals an interesting contrast between the two companies heading into earnings.
As of October 19, SPCX’s 30-day 25-delta puts carried approximately 4.56 volatility points of premium over comparable calls, versus 2.48 points for TSLA. This suggests relatively stronger demand for downside protection in SpaceX.
Both stocks also exhibit inverted volatility term structures, with near-term options carrying elevated premiums ahead of earnings.
SpotGamma Compass: Relative Upside Potential
The SpotGamma Compass Map places both stocks in the lower-left quadrant, reflecting midrange implied volatility ranks and relatively low risk reversal ranks.
This positioning suggests that upside options may offer more favorable relative pricing, although neither stock exhibits exceptionally cheap volatility. TSLA sits slightly farther toward the upside-potential side of the Compass than SPCX.
Importantly, the Compass measures relative options pricing, not the probability of a bullish earnings reaction.
SpotGamma Compass Map — TSLA and SPCX Relative Upside Potential
Dealer Gamma: TSLA Faces Greater Volatility Risk
The gamma maps highlight another important distinction.
SPCX: Substantial positive gamma concentrations around $155–$170, particularly near $160, suggest dealer hedging could help stabilize prices and suppress volatility following earnings. However, negative gamma builds above $180, potentially amplifying upside momentum if shares break through the positive gamma region. The $195 High Volatility Point marks an important upper volatility reference.
SPCX Synthetic Dealer Gamma Exposure — $146 Low Volatility Point
TSLA: Dealer gamma shows a significant shift from yesterday’s negative gamma environment toward predominantly positive gamma exposure, suggesting greater potential for price stabilization heading into earnings. With shares last closing near $368, substantial positive gamma concentrations around $370–$380 could help dampen volatility, while the newly established $390 Low Volatility Point marks the peak of aggregate positive gamma exposure and a potential stabilization zone.
However, notable negative gamma pockets remain near $350, $385, and $400, where hedging activity could amplify localized price swings.
TSLA Synthetic Dealer Gamma Exposure — $390 High Volatility Point
TSLA appears more vulnerable to an amplified directional move, while SPCX has a more balanced gamma profile with identifiable areas of potential stabilization and acceleration. These synthetic positioning estimates are not confirmed dealer inventories.
Merger speculation could also keep volatility elevated beyond the initial reports, potentially limiting the usual post-earnings IV collapse.
4. The Merger Wildcard: Could SpaceX Buy Tesla?
The potential combination of Tesla and SpaceX has attracted renewed attention following Barclays’ analysis suggesting that an announcement could arrive ahead of Tesla’s December 3 annual shareholder meeting.
The bank has outlined a potential all-stock structure with SpaceX as the acquirer, although neither company has confirmed a transaction or publicly established deal terms.
From an investment perspective, a merger would create exposure to an enormous collection of businesses spanning electric vehicles, robotics, autonomous transportation, satellite communications, launch services and AI infrastructure.
However, the combined capital requirements would be equally significant.
For options traders, there are three major considerations.
- Correlation risk: A merger-related announcement could create sharp, interconnected moves in both securities, potentially reducing diversification benefits. The direction and magnitude would depend heavily on transaction terms and relative valuations.
- Gap risk: A credible announcement could generate a move well beyond the options-implied ranges, particularly if proposed transaction terms materially change the market’s valuation assumptions.
- Volatility persistence: Even without an announcement, continued speculation could support longer-dated options premiums after quarterly earnings uncertainty has passed.
A merger is not a confirmed outcome, and its eventual impact would depend heavily on valuation, exchange ratios, dilution and shareholder approval.
5. Three Potential Trading Scenarios
Bullish: Strong Earnings Fuel a Breakout
Better-than-expected SpaceX results Tuesday could establish positive momentum heading into Tesla’s Wednesday report. Improving Tesla margins or encouraging Robotaxi developments could push shares beyond their upper implied ranges, with negative dealer gamma potentially accelerating the move.
Neutral: Results Meet Expectations
If neither company delivers a major surprise or merger update, both stocks could remain within their implied ranges. Short-dated implied volatility would likely decline, benefiting premium sellers, although lingering merger speculation could limit the volatility reset.
Bearish: Capital Spending Raises Concerns
Disappointing SpaceX cash flow or higher AI spending guidance, followed by weaker Tesla margins, could pressure both stocks. A breakdown through key negative gamma regions could reinforce downside momentum as dealer hedging flows amplify selling.
6. The Options Trader’s Takeaway
SpaceX’s Tuesday results may influence expectations for Tesla before Tesla reports Wednesday, potentially changing both directional positioning and options pricing.
Rather than chasing expensive outright options ahead of either announcement, defined-risk vertical spreads may offer a more controlled way to express a directional view.
Potential Trade Ideas
TSLA’s gamma profile suggests greater potential for volatility expansion, while SPCX’s more balanced positioning and relatively expensive downside protection favor a different approach.
Two defined-risk options structures worth considering are a bullish call debit spread in TSLA and a put credit spread in SPCX.
TSLA: October 23 $380/$400 Bull Call Spread
At a $6.25 debit, this $20-wide spread risks $625 to potentially earn $1,375, offering approximately 2.2:1 maximum reward-to-risk with a $386.25 expiration breakeven.
The setup provides bullish exposure to a potential earnings breakout, particularly if TSLA pushes through its $390 High Volatility Point. Maximum profit requires shares to reach $400 or higher at expiration.
SPCX: October 23 $145/$135 Bull Put Spread
At a $3.35 credit, this spread offers $335 maximum profit against $665 maximum risk, with a $141.65 expiration breakeven.
The strategy benefits from elevated downside premiums and a neutral-to-bullish reaction, but negative gamma concentrated near $140–$145 introduces meaningful downside gap risk.
For traders seeking additional time, November 6 or November 20 expiration spreads offer alternatives, although the premiums and reward-to-risk profiles will differ.
Both examples use midday Tuesday indicative pricing and should be reassessed against live quotes before entry. The TSLA debit spread provides bullish convexity but is not a pure long-gamma trade across all prices; the SPCX credit spread generally carries short-gamma exposure.
Bottom line: The options market is pricing substantial moves in both stocks, but the combination of earnings, merger speculation, and contrasting gamma profiles creates opportunities for volatility to exceed expectations. The most important signals may emerge as dealer positioning and implied volatility adjust after each report.

sources.news_title: Tesla SpaceX Merger Odds Hit 56% by May 2027 on Kalshi
sources.text:
Kalshi traders put a Tesla SpaceX merger at 56% before May 2027 and only 11% before the end of this month, and both companies report earnings inside the next 48 hours. The market has taken about $1.67 million in volume and did most of its repricing in the week of 13 October, after Barclays raised the prospect of an announcement within weeks.
Scale is what has turned a recurring piece of speculation into a live question for both shareholder bases. SpaceX carries a $2.01 trillion valuation against Tesla’s $1.46 trillion, and it spent $15.8 billion on AI capacity in the second quarter alone while Tesla is burning cash to keep pace. The two sets of numbers land on consecutive evenings, which is why a Tesla SpaceX merger is the question hanging over both calls.
Nothing has been filed on either side that would start a formal Tesla SpaceX merger process. No merger agreement, no special committee and no regulatory submission exists, and ARK Invest said plainly in its own valuation work that its Tesla model treats the company as standalone.
Kalshi Prices a Tesla SpaceX Merger at 11% This Month and 56% by May 2027
The contract ladder is the part worth reading rather than any single headline number. Kalshi quoted 42% before 1 March 2027, 49% before 1 April and 56% before 1 May at midday on Tuesday, with the near-dated contract on a combination before 1 November sitting at 11%. Traders are pricing a Tesla SpaceX merger that arrives eventually rather than one that arrives this quarter.
All three dated contracts repriced in the week of 13 October, climbing from the low 30s and low 40s to a peak near 59% before giving back part of the move. Kalshi’s rules set a high bar for any of them to pay out, requiring a definitive, binding agreement announced through official channels, and they state that a comment from Musk counts only if it amounts to “an unambiguous, affirmative confirmation of a definitive signed agreement.”
Investor Takeaway
Kalshi prices a Tesla SpaceX merger at 11% before 1 November against 56% before May 2027, so the money is on a slow deal rather than an imminent one.
SpaceX Reports Tuesday Night and Tesla Follows on Wednesday
SpaceX publishes third quarter results after the close on Tuesday, its second report as a public company, with Tesla following on Wednesday, Reuters reported. Analysts polled by LSEG expect SpaceX revenue of about $12.74 billion and earnings of 14 cents a share, against Tesla’s adjusted 43 cents on roughly $27.88 billion. Options on SpaceX imply a 7.8% move either way, a range of $134.64 to $157.42, and Tesla SpaceX merger questions are likely on both calls.
Capital spending is the line both of these reports are going to turn on. SpaceX put $15.8 billion into AI capacity in the second quarter alone, and Evercore ISI expects about $151 billion of capex in 2027 against an exit-2026 annualized revenue run rate near $104 billion. Tesla will spend more than $25 billion this year and analysts expect negative free cash flow of $4.92 billion for the quarter, after a delivery beat of 486,532 vehicles that has not stopped the stock falling about 17% in 2026.
Barclays Put a Tesla SpaceX Merger Before the 3 December Annual Meeting
Barclays told clients a deal could be announced before Tesla’s annual meeting on 3 December, with SpaceX the likelier acquirer of the two. Under an all-stock structure the bank sketched, Musk would hold about 37% of the combined equity and 56% of the votes, which keeps control without requiring him to buy it.
The market capitalizations of the two companies already point in the same direction. SpaceX closed Monday at $147.96 for a $2.01 trillion valuation, against Tesla at $368.99 and $1.46 trillion in Tuesday morning trade. Shawn Campbell of Camelthorn Investments, who owns both, told Reuters a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla “would be cleaner,” partly because it would leave the China business as a separate asset to handle.
ARK Models $3.8 Trillion of Combined Revenue by 2031
ARK Invest published a Tesla valuation on 19 October putting the shares at about $4,400 by 2031, with a $5,000 bull case and $3,300 bear case, and put a Tesla SpaceX merger inside its five-year horizon. Tasha Keeney and Daniel Maguire estimate the two together would generate $3.8 trillion of revenue and $2.7 trillion of EBIT by 2031.
The split inside those numbers matters more than the total for anyone thinking about an exchange ratio. SpaceX would contribute roughly 62% of the revenue and 69% of the EBIT, which puts the rocket and connectivity business ahead of the carmaker on both lines by the end of the decade. ARK built the price target without the deal, so the combined figures sit alongside the model rather than inside it.
Investor Takeaway
ARK’s $4,400 Tesla target excludes any Tesla SpaceX merger, so the combined $3.8 trillion scenario is additional to the price target rather than the basis for it.
Musk Has Not Confirmed a Process and Only the xAI Deal Has Closed
Musk declined to rule out a combination on the July earnings call while saying it would need “the appropriate process,” and the arithmetic of what Tesla holders would need to accept has not changed since. SpaceX absorbed xAI in February before its June listing, which is the only Musk consolidation that has actually closed. That transaction combined two private companies four months before SpaceX listed, a lighter process than merging two public shareholder registers and two boards.
The bull and bear ranges on SpaceX and Tesla still model the two names apart, and a Tesla SpaceX merger would force both sets of numbers to be rebuilt from the exchange ratio up. Until a definitive agreement exists, Tuesday and Wednesday are the only scheduled moments at which either management can say something that moves the Kalshi ladder.
